title: Pulmonary Artery Systolic Pressure Response to Exercise in Patients with Rheumatic Mitral Stenosis: Determinants and Prognostic Value.
text_ai: Pulmonary hypertension in response to exercise is a marker of the hemodynamic severity of mitral stenosis (MS). However, the factors related to elevated pulmonary pressure with exercise are not well defined. The aim of this study was to assess the parameters associated with the pulmonary pressure response to exercise in patients with pure rheumatic MS. Methods: This prospective, single-center study enrolled consecutive adults with pure rheumatic MS and preserved LV systolic function who underwent comprehensive echocardiography at rest and during standardized exercise on a semi-supine cycle ergometer. Mitral valve area by planimetry, mean transmitral gradient, left atrial (LA) volume index, and indices of LV diastolic function were recorded. Pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP) was calculated from the tricuspid regurgitant jet and estimated right atrial pressure. Exercise protocol targeted at least 85% of predicted maximum heart rate. Peak PASP (PASP_peak) and the change from rest (ΔPASP) were derived. An abnormal exercise pulmonary pressure response was defined as PASP_peak ≥60 mmHg or ΔPASP ≥40 mmHg. Patients were followed for major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE: all-cause death, hospitalization for heart failure, or mitral valve intervention). Multivariable linear regression identified determinants of PASP_peak, while Cox models evaluated the prognostic value of exercise PASP after adjustment for resting PASP, MS severity, age, sex, and comorbidity burden. Results: Among 128 patients, 62 (48%) exhibited an abnormal exercise PASP response. PASP_peak correlated inversely with MV area (r = -0.42, p<0.001) and positively with LA volume index (r = 0.46, p<0.001) and E/e' (r = 0.44, p<0.001). In multivariable analysis, smaller MV area (β = -0.29, p = 0.002), higher E/e' (β = 0.26, p = 0.005), and larger LA volume index (β = 0.22, p = 0.01) independently predicted higher PASP_peak. Over a median follow-up of 3.1 years, 15 MACE occurred. Exercise PASP_peak ≥60 mmHg was associated with increased MACE risk (adjusted HR 2.8, 95% CI 1.4–5.7, p=0.003), independent of resting PASP and MS severity. The addition of PASP_peak to a baseline model improved discrimination (C-statistic 0.74 to 0.81, p=0.02) and net reclassification (NRI 0.27, p=0.01). Conclusion: In pure rheumatic MS, the pulmonary pressure response to exercise is determined by MV area, LV diastolic pressures, and LA remodeling, and carries incremental prognostic information beyond resting hemodynamics. Incorporating exercise PASP assessment may enhance risk stratification and guide timing of valve intervention.
prefix: Pulmonary hypertension in response to exercise is a marker of the hemodynamic severity of mitral stenosis (MS). However, the factors related to elevated pulmonary pressure with exercise are not well defined. The aim of this study was to assess the parameters associated with the pulmonary pressure response to exercise in patients with pure rheumatic MS.

title: Fast rotating Bose-Einstein condensates in an asymmetric trap
text_ai: We investigate the effect of the anisotropy of a harmonic trap on the behaviour of a fast rotating Bose-Einstein condensate. This is done in the framework of the 2D Gross-Pitaevskii equation and requires a symplectic reduction of the quadratic form defining the energy. Within this reduced framework we derive an effective 2D energy on the reduced phase space that encodes anisotropy through a modified metric and magnetic potential. In the fast-rotation limit the dynamics are governed by a deformed lowest Landau level structure; the resulting functional admits minimizers with elongated condensates and vortex rows aligned along the weak-confinement axis. We prove energy bounds that match the LLL asymptotics up to a correction determined by the ellipticity and interaction strength. The macroscopic profile and vortex density are described by a reduced Thomas–Fermi description compatible with an anisotropic trap; numerical simulations of the full 2D GPE corroborate the predicted lattice distortion and the shift of the critical rotation frequency for vortex nucleation. Our results clarify how trap ellipticity reshapes the vortex matter in fast-rotating quantum fluids and related experiments.
prefix: We investigate the effect of the anisotropy of a harmonic trap on the behaviour of a fast rotating Bose-Einstein condensate. This is done in the framework of the 2D Gross-Pitaevskii equation and requires a symplectic reduction of the quadratic form defining the energy.

title: Prognosis of French COVID-19 patients with chronic liver disease: A national retrospective cohort study for 2020.
text_ai: The impact of chronic liver disease on outcomes in patients with COVID-19 is uncertain. Hence, we aimed to explore this association. We explored the outcomes of all adult inpatients with COVID-19 in France, in 2020. We computed adjusted odds ratios to measure the associations between chronic liver disease, alcohol use disorders, mechanical ventilation and day-30 in-hospital mortality. Methods: We conducted a nationwide retrospective cohort using the French national hospital discharge database (PMSI) for 2020. Adult inpatients (≥18 years) with a coded SARS-CoV-2 infection admitted in 2020 were included. Chronic liver disease (CLD) was defined by ICD-10 codes K70–K77 and F10.x for alcohol use disorders (AUD). Cirrhosis was identified by K74.x or related codes; non-cirrhotic CLD encompassed remaining chronic liver disease without cirrhosis. The primary outcome was day-30 in-hospital mortality. A secondary outcome was receipt of invasive mechanical ventilation. Multivariable logistic regression with hospital-level random intercepts estimated adjusted odds ratios (aORs), controlling for age, sex, Charlson comorbidity index, obesity, diabetes, hypertension, chronic kidney disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, cancer, liver failure, and antiviral therapies where applicable. We performed stratified analyses by cirrhosis status and tested multiplicative interactions between CLD and AUD. Missing data were addressed by multiple imputation; sensitivity analyses used complete-case analyses. Results: Among approximately 130,000 eligible admissions, CLD was present in 8,470 (6.5%), including 2,150 with cirrhosis and 6,320 without cirrhosis. AUD was documented in 3,760 (2.9%). Day-30 mortality was 13.8%; invasive mechanical ventilation occurred in 10.5%. After adjustment, CLD was associated with higher day-30 mortality (aOR 1.31, 95% CI 1.25–1.37). AUD conferred increased mortality risk (aOR 1.18, 95% CI 1.12–1.25). Mechanical ventilation was more frequent among those with CLD (aOR 1.25, 95% CI 1.15–1.37) and AUD (aOR 1.12, 95% CI 1.05–1.20). Stratified analyses showed greater mortality risk with cirrhosis (aOR 1.58, 95% CI 1.46–1.72) than non-cirrhotic CLD (aOR 1.14, 95% CI 1.07–1.22). The combined exposure to CLD and AUD yielded higher odds (aOR 1.54, 95% CI 1.38–1.72) with a significant interaction (P-interaction <0.01). Findings were consistent across imputations and complete-case analyses. Conclusions: In this national French cohort, CLD, particularly cirrhosis, independently increased the risk of day-30 in-hospital mortality and of invasive ventilation among adults hospitalized for COVID-19, with augmentation when AUD was present. These results support targeted risk stratification and may inform resource allocation and preventive strategies for patients with CLD during ongoing and future SARS-CoV-2 waves.
prefix: The impact of chronic liver disease on outcomes in patients with COVID-19 is uncertain. Hence, we aimed to explore this association. We explored the outcomes of all adult inpatients with COVID-19 in France, in 2020. We computed adjusted odds ratios to measure the associations between chronic liver disease, alcohol use disorders, mechanical ventilation and day-30 in-hospital mortality.

title: The orbital structure of a tidally induced bar
text_ai: Orbits are the key building blocks of any density distribution and their study helps us understand the kinematical structure and the evolution of galaxies. Here we investigate orbits in a tidally induced bar of a dwarf galaxy, using an $N$-body simulation of an initially disky dwarf galaxy orbiting a Milky Way-like host. Orbits were tracked for stars currently occupying the bar region, and the potential was reconstructed from the N-body snapshot at multiple phases of the interaction to probe both the growth and the quasi-steady state of the structure. Orbits were integrated in the rotating frame with the instantaneous potential and analyzed with a combination of Fourier spectral analysis, Lyapunov exponents, and surfaces of section to identify regular resonant families (planar x1-like orbits and 3D vertical resonances such as x1v1) and to quantify chaoticity. We thus classify orbits as regular x1- and box/loop-type members, vertically extended resonant families, or chaotic. The inner bar is predominantly supported by planar x1-like families elongated along the bar, comprising roughly half to two-thirds of bar particles depending on epoch. A substantial fraction of vertically extended resonant orbits (x1v1 and related 3D families) contribute to a modest boxy/peanut signature, most evident when the tidal forcing peaks near pericentre. A population of chaotic orbits becomes appreciable, particularly near corotation, where the time-dependent tides amplify diffusion in frequency space. Compared to bars grown in isolation, the tidally induced bar shows a higher chaotic fraction and a somewhat more diffuse distribution of stable regular families, yet a robust backbone of x1-like support persists. The orbital structure thus links the transient tidal stirring to the observed kinematic imprints in dwarfs on eccentric orbits.
prefix: Orbits are the key building blocks of any density distribution and their study helps us understand the kinematical structure and the evolution of galaxies. Here we investigate orbits in a tidally induced bar of a dwarf galaxy, using an $N$-body simulation of an initially disky dwarf galaxy orbiting a Milky Way-like host.

title: Two-scale momentum theory for time-dependent modelling of large wind farms
text_ai: This paper presents a theory based on the law of momentum conservation to define and help analyse the problem of large wind farm aerodynamics. This two-scale formulation partitions the flow into a rotor-dominated near-field and a far-field farm-scale region, with rotor-scale momentum extraction parameterized by a time-dependent thrust coefficient and the farm-scale deficit represented as a spatially averaged drag. Starting from the instantaneous momentum equations and invoking horizontal homogeneity within the farm, we obtain a coupled system for the farm-scale mean wind speed U_f(t) and an integral measure of rotor induction a(t). The rotor-budget yields T_r(t) = 0.5 ρ A_t C_T(U_r,t) U_r^2, where U_r is the effective rotor inflow and C_T encodes the dynamic response of induction, stall and yaw. The farm-budget expresses the total turbine loading as T_f(t) = 0.5 ρ A_eff C_f(U_f) U_f^2, with A_eff the cross-sectional area times turbine density and C_f an effective farm-coefficient that captures wake interaction and recovery. The two equations are coupled through U_r = U_f + ΔU_r and through the dependence of C_f on layout, density and time-varying CT. The resulting system, though low-dimensional, retains the essential physics of two-scale momentum extraction and wakes, and provides a transparent framework for time-dependent analysis. In limiting cases, it reduces to classical momentum theory for isolated turbines and to a steady, grid-scale drag law for dense arrays. Validation against large-eddy simulations and field data demonstrates accuracy for representative layouts and inflow trajectories, and the approach offers a computationally efficient tool for design optimization, control, and real-time forecasting of large wind-farm performance.
prefix: This paper presents a theory based on the law of momentum conservation to define and help analyse the problem of large wind farm aerodynamics.

title: Leveraging Semantic Representations Combined with Contextual Word Representations for Recognizing Textual Entailment in Vietnamese
text_ai: RTE is a significant problem and is a reasonably active research community. The proposed research works on the approach to this problem are pretty diverse with many different directions. For Vietnamese, the RTE problem is moderately new, but this problem plays a vital role in natural language understanding systems. To address Vietnamese RTE, we design a hybrid architecture that fuses symbolic semantic representations with contextual embeddings. Semantic representations capture lexical relations, predicate-argument structures, and constraints derived from a Vietnamese semantic network and multilingual resources projected into a joint space. Contextual representations are produced by a pre-trained Vietnamese transformer that encodes sentence-level nuances and discourse cues. The two channels are integrated through a cross-attention fusion module and an entailment classifier trained with a margin objective. We introduce a bilingual alignment strategy using cross-lingual supervision, augmenting training with synthetic paraphrases. Experimental results on a Vietnamese RTE corpus show gains over baselines using either semantic features or contextual embeddings alone. Ablation studies reveal the complementary strength of the combined representation, particularly in cases involving lexical ambiguity and paraphrase variation.

For Vietnamese, the RTE problem is moderately new, but this problem plays a vital role in natural language understanding systems.

title: Binary Black-box Evasion Attacks Against Deep Learning-based Static Malware Detectors with Adversarial Byte-Level Language Model
text_ai: Anti-malware engines are the first line of defense against malicious software. While widely used, feature engineering-based anti-malware engines are vulnerable to unseen (zero-day) attacks. Recently, deep learning-based static anti-malware detectors have achieved success in identifying unseen attacks without requiring feature engineering and dynamic analysis. Here, we introduce a binary black-box evasion paradigm that leverages a byte-level adversarial language model to generate perturbations that preserve functionality in the byte stream. The attack operates under query budgets and relies on a surrogate model trained through limited interactions with the detector to steer perturbations while constraining validity and runtime behavior. We cast the problem as a constrained, gradient-free optimization over byte sequences, with the adversarial LM producing candidate byte replacements and insertions that preserve functionality but perturb classifier inputs. We evaluate against multiple deep learning–based static detectors on portable executable samples, achieving high evasion rates with minimal byte-level modifications and without deteriorating execution. Results show transferability across detectors and implications for defender resilience. We conclude with mitigation strategies including robust training, input normalization, and certified defenses against byte-level perturbations.

Recently, deep learning-based static anti-malware detectors have achieved success in identifying unseen attacks without requiring feature engineering and dynamic analysis.

title: Transcriptional Similarity in Couples Reveals the Impact of Shared Environment and Lifestyle on Gene Regulation through Modified Cytosines
text_ai: Gene expression is a complex and quantitative trait that is influenced by both genetic and non-genetic regulators including environmental factors. Evaluating the contribution of environment to gene expression regulation and identifying which genes are more likely to be influenced by environmental factors are important for understanding human complex traits. To quantify this contribution, we assembled a cohort of adult couples and performed paired transcriptome profiling in peripheral blood mononuclear cells, together with genome-wide maps of cytosine modifications (5mC and 5hmC) using complementary bisulfite- and oxidative-bisulfite-based sequencing. We then used linear mixed-effects models to decompose transcript-level covariation into components attributable to shared environment, genetic background, and idiosyncratic factors, while adjusting for cell-type composition and age. We observed substantially higher transcriptional similarity within couples than between unrelated individuals, with a large portion of this similarity linked to concordant patterns of cytosine modification at promoter and enhancer regions. Genes showing strong environment-associated coexpression were enriched for metabolic and immune pathways, consistent with lifestyle- and diet-mediated regulation. Mediation analyses indicated that cytosine modifications partially mediate the relationship between shared lifestyle factors (diet quality, smoking, physical activity) and gene expression, suggesting a mechanistic role for epigenetic marks in transducing environmental exposure into transcriptional changes. Longitudinal subsampling confirmed persistence of these patterns over months, supporting an enduring epigenetic signature of shared living. Collectively, our results implicate modified cytosines as central mediators of environmental influence on transcription and highlight the relevance of non-genetic inheritance in shaping gene regulation.
prefix: Gene expression is a complex and quantitative trait that is influenced by both genetic and non-genetic regulators including environmental factors. Evaluating the contribution of environment to gene expression regulation and identifying which genes are more likely to be influenced by environmental factors are important for understanding human complex traits.

title: Characterising the VHE diffuse emission in the central 200 parsecs of our Galaxy with H.E.S.S
text_ai: The diffuse very high-energy (VHE, > 100 GeV) gamma-ray emission observed in the central 200 pc of the Milky Way by H.E.S.S. was found to follow the dense matter distribution in the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) up to a longitudinal distance of about 130 pc to the Galactic Centre (GC), where the flux rapidly decreases. To characterize its origin and transport properties, we perform a joint spatial-spectral analysis of the diffuse emission using a template-based maximum-likelihood fit to the H.E.S.S. data, in concert with high-resolution gas tracers of the CMZ (e.g., CS and CO maps) to trace the target material. The modeling includes a dedicated leptonic component for inverse-Compton emission, calibrated with multiwavelength templates, and accounts for the contribution of unresolved point sources through simulations of the instrument point-spread function and population studies of the inner Galaxy. Data are binned in energy to track spectral variations, and systematics from the background estimation, gas tracers, and instrument response are propagated to the final results. We find that the diffuse component remains tightly correlated with the dense CMZ gas out to ∼130 pc from the GC, and cannot be explained by a spatially uniform local CR density alone. Instead, the data require a CR density that is enhanced with respect to the local solar neighborhood by a factor of a few, with a modest radial gradient toward the GC. The reconstructed emissivity profile and the CMZ-correlated morphology strongly favor a hadronic origin for the bulk of the diffuse emission, with a subdominant, spatially structured leptonic contribution consistent with the overall multiwavelength constraints. The integrated spectrum of the diffuse component is well described by a power law in the 0.3–40 TeV range, with an index Γ ≈ 2.3–2.5 and no clear cut-off up to the highest energies probed, implying acceleration of protons to at least tens of TeV within the central few hundred parsecs. The radial and spectral information constrain the CR transport properties in the CMZ, indicating diffusion that is suppressed relative to the local interstellar medium by a factor of a few, compatible with enhanced magnetic turbulence and gas density. Collectively, these results support a scenario in which CRs accelerated in the GC region fill the CMZ, interact with dense gas, and give rise to the observed diffuse VHE emission, with the emission fading beyond the 130 pc extent set by the gas distribution and CR transport.

title: Epidemiology of Injuries in National Collegiate Athletic Association Women's Lacrosse: 2014-2015 Through 2018-2019.
text_ai: Lacrosse is an increasingly popular sport; the number of teams participating in collegiate women's lacrosse has increased by 21.4% in the past 5 years. The growth of National Collegiate Athletic Association women's lacrosse, coupled with the ongoing discussions surrounding protective equipment, necessitates further epidemiologic studies in this population. Using NCAA Injury Surveillance Program data from 2014-2015 through 2018-2019, we estimated injury rate per 1000 athlete-exposures and by game versus practice exposure. Injury etiologies, anatomical sites, and severity were summarized, with estimates stratified by playing position, session, and year. In-season injuries predominated and contact-related mechanisms accounted for the majority of injuries in games; noncontact injuries were more common in practices. The knee and ankle were most frequently injured, followed by the head/face. Concussions and mild-to-moderate injuries comprised a substantial proportion of total injuries, though time lost varied by category. Protective equipment usage patterns correlated with reduced risk for specific injuries but not uniformly across all categories. These trends highlight prevention opportunities, particularly in neurosafety protocols and ankle-stability programs, and in evaluating equipment standards for women's lacrosse.
prefix: Lacrosse is an increasingly popular sport; the number of teams participating in collegiate women's lacrosse has increased by 21.4% in the past 5 years. The growth of National Collegiate Athletic Association women's lacrosse, coupled with the ongoing discussions surrounding protective equipment, necessitates further epidemiologic studies in this population.

title: Efficacy of the combination of modern medicine and traditional Chinese medicine in pulmonary fibrosis arising as a sequelae in convalescent COVID-19 patients: a randomized multicenter trial.
text_ai: The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV-2) has led to a significant number of mortalities worldwide. COVID-19 poses a serious threat to human life. The clinical manifestations of COVID-19 are diverse and severe and 20% of infected patients are reported to be in a critical condition. In survivors, fibrotic sequelae with persistent dyspnea and reduced diffusion capacity have emerged as a major contributor to ongoing morbidity. This randomized multicenter trial evaluated whether an integrative strategy combining modern medicine with traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) could halt or reverse fibrotic progression and improve functional status in convalescent patients with post-COVID-19 pulmonary fibrosis. Methods: Adults with prior laboratory-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection and radiographic evidence of pulmonary fibrosis 3–6 months after hospital discharge were randomized 1:1 at 12 centers to receive standard post-COVID care (including rehabilitation and, when indicated, antifibrotic therapy) or the same standard care plus a standardized oral TCM formulation (a 12-herb decoction) administered twice daily for 24 weeks, with optional acupuncture sessions weekly for the first 12 weeks. The primary endpoint was the absolute change in forced vital capacity (FVC) percent predicted from baseline to Week 24. Secondary endpoints included diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) percent predicted, HRCT fibrosis score, 6-minute walk distance (6MWD), quality of life (SF-36 and St George’s Respiratory Questionnaire), and safety/tolerability. Results: Of 320 randomized participants (mean age 56 years; 58% male), 312 completed Week 24 assessments. The integrative therapy produced a greater improvement in FVC% predicted than standard care alone (Δ 6.2% vs 1.8%; between-group difference 4.4 percentage points; P<0.001). DLCO improved more with the integrative approach (Δ 7.5% vs 2.3%; P=0.002). HRCT fibrosis scores declined modestly in both groups but favored integrative therapy (−2.1 vs −0.3 points; P=0.01). 6MWD increased by 48 m in the integrative group versus 15 m in controls (P=0.006). Quality-of-life assessments demonstrated greater gains in physical functioning and symptom burden with the combination therapy. Adverse events were comparable between groups (12% vs 11%), with no signal of hepatotoxicity or other organ toxicity attributable to the TCM regimen; laboratory abnormalities remained within acceptable limits. Conclusions: In convalescent COVID-19 patients with post-infectious pulmonary fibrosis, adding a standardized TCM regimen to modern medical therapy yielded superior improvements in lung function, radiographic trajectory, and exercise capacity, with an acceptable safety profile. These findings support further confirmatory trials and longer-term follow-up to determine durability and generalizability across populations.

COVID-19 poses a serious threat to human life. The clinical manifestations of COVID-19 are diverse and severe and 20% of infected patients are reported to be in a critical condition.

title: AutoPET Challenge: Combining nn-Unet with Swin UNETR Augmented by Maximum Intensity Projection Classifier
text_ai: Tumor volume and changes in tumor characteristics over time are important biomarkers for cancer therapy. In this context, FDG-PET/CT scans are routinely used for staging and re-staging of cancer, as the radiolabeled fluorodeoxyglucose is taken up in regions of high metabolism. To this end, we propose a synergistic pipeline that fuses a high-precision segmentation backbone (nnUNet) with a global-context transformer (Swin UNETR) and a compact Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) classifier for lesion-level refinement. The MIP classifier operates on 2D projections derived from PET volumes to provide a fast, location-agnostic prior that guides the segmentation head and suppresses isolated false positives. Training uses multi-site AutoPET data with voxel- and lesion-level annotations; optimization employs a composite loss combining Dice, focal, and cross-entropy terms, plus test-time augmentation and snapshot ensembling. Evaluation reports voxel-wise Dice and lesion-wise metrics (sensitivity, specificity, and false positives per study). Across five-fold cross-validation, the method achieves Dice 0.74 ± 0.09 and lesion-level sensitivity 0.86, with 0.65 FP per scan, outperforming the single-model baselines by a notable margin. The approach demonstrates robustness across scanners and disease sites and runs within practical inference times for prospective deployment.

title: Chronotaraxis as a harbinger of medial thalamic infarction.
text_ai: Chronotaraxis is an impairment of the perception of the sequencing of time. This alteration of temporality has been described as being characteristically associated with thalamic involvement, specifically in the dorsomedial nucleus. We report the clinical cases of two patients with acute ischaemic strokes located in said territory, with a clinical presentation based on this symptom and the recognition of which was essential in the therapeutic approach. Methods: We report two cases of acute ischaemic stroke confined to the dorsomedial nucleus who presented with chronotaraxis as a prominent initial symptom. Diagnostic workup included diffusion-weighted MRI and perfusion imaging to delineate infarct core and penumbra, vascular imaging to exclude large vessel occlusion, and standard etiologic assessment (ECG, telemetry, laboratory tests). Chronotaraxis was assessed with a concise bedside protocol evaluating temporal ordering, duration estimation, and prospective timing during the first 72 hours, repeated during the subacute phase. Neuropsychological assessment focused on executive function, memory, and orientation, with particular attention to temporal consciousness. All patients received guideline-concordant acute stroke care and targeted rehabilitation. Results: Case 1 involved a 67-year-old man with abrupt, disproportionate difficulty in sequencing recent events and estimating short intervals, accompanied by preserved language and visual-spatial skills. MRI demonstrated an acute diffusion restriction isolated to the right mediodorsal nucleus, with no occlusive large vessel disease. Case 2 concerned a 58-year-old woman who reported a similar disturbance in the perception of time, misjudging interval lengths and the order of consecutive actions; imaging revealed an acute infarct in the left dorsomedial nucleus. Both patients lacked profound hemispheric deficits and had stable gait; there were no secondary lesions. Acute management adhered to stroke guidelines, including antiplatelet therapy and risk-factor optimization, alongside early cognitive and occupational therapy aimed at temporal processing and executive strategies. Chronotaraxis improved progressively over days in both cases, with gradual restoration of temporal sequencing and interval perception. At 3-month follow-up, both patients achieved functional independence for activities of daily living; one retained subtle, task-specific difficulties in complex temporal planning, whereas the other showed near-complete restoration of temporal perception with minor residual sequencing challenges. Conclusions: Chronotaraxis can constitute a salient, early manifestation of medial thalamic infarction and should prompt prompt MRI-focused evaluation of the dorsomedial nucleus. Recognition facilitates timely diagnosis, risk-factor management, and targeted neurorehabilitation, underscoring the critical role of thalamo-prefrontal networks in temporal cognition.
prefix: Chronotaraxis is an impairment of the perception of the sequencing of time. This alteration of temporality has been described as being characteristically associated with thalamic involvement, specifically in the dorsomedial nucleus. We report the clinical cases of two patients with acute ischaemic strokes located in said territory, with a clinical presentation based on this symptom and the recognition of which was essential in the therapeutic approach.

title: The role of ambient temperature and body mass on body temperature, standard metabolic rate and evaporative water loss in southern African anurans of different habitat specialisation.
text_ai: Temperature and water availability are two of the most important variables affecting all aspects of an anuran's key physiological processes such as body temperature ( T b ), evaporative water loss (EWL) and standard metabolic rate (SMR). Across six southern African anuran species representing aquatic, terrestrial and fossorial specialists, we exposed adults to a range of ambient temperatures (Ta) under controlled humidity to quantify how Ta and body mass (MB) shape body temperature (Tb), evaporative water loss (EWL) and standard metabolic rate (SMR). Tb was measured with implanted micro-thermistors, SMR with open-flow respirometry (VO2) after fasting, and EWL gravimetrically during stable humidity trials (60–65%). We applied linear mixed-effects models to test the main effects and interactions of Ta, MB, guild (habitat specialization) and their two- and three-way interactions on each response variable, with species and experimental run as random effects. Tb increased with Ta across all taxa, but the slope of Ta–Tb relationships varied with MB and guild. Terrestrial and fossorial specialists showed steeper Tb responses to increasing Ta than aquatic taxa, indicating lesser buffering of body heat in drier, structurally heterogeneous microhabitats. MB modulated these responses: smaller individuals tended to exhibit larger Tb per degree rise in Ta, whereas larger-bodied taxa displayed attenuated Tb increments at high Ta, consistent with differential surface-area-to-volume constraints and thermal inertia among guilds. SMR rose with MB (scaling exponent near 0.70) and was positively related to Ta, with Q10 values averaging ~2.2 across the 15–25°C range and slightly lower (≈2.0) from 25–35°C, but with guild-specific deviations. EWL increased with Ta and decreased humidity, scaling with MB close to surface-area expectations (exponent ≈0.66). Terrestrial and fossorial species exhibited higher absolute EWL at elevated Ta than aquatic congeners, likely reflecting greater skin permeability and reduced reliance on ambient aquatic environments for hydration; humidity modulated EWL such that arid trials amplified the Ta-driven EWL response. In all species, mass-corrected EWL rose with Ta more steeply in smaller individuals within each guild, highlighting distinct evaporative strategies aligned with habitat specialization. Together, these results indicate that ambient temperature and body mass jointly constrain Tb, SMR and EWL in southern African anurans, with habitat specialization mediating the strength and direction of these relationships. The findings imply divergent vulnerability to warming and fluctuating water availability across guilds, with terrestrial and fossorial taxa potentially facing greater evaporative and energetic costs under future climate scenarios, whereas aquatic specialists may experience buffering of Tb but persistent water-balance challenges.

title: Generative AI models enable efficient and physically consistent sea-ice simulations
text_ai: Sea ice is governed by highly complex, scale-invariant, and anisotropic processes that are challenging to represent in Earth system models. While advanced numerical models have improved our understanding of the sea-ice dynamics, their computational costs often limit their application in ensemble forecasting and climate simulations. Here, we introduce a generative surrogate capable of producing physically plausible sea-ice fields conditioned on prognostic state, forcing, and metadata. The model is trained on high-fidelity simulations spanning representative thermodynamic regimes and floe dynamics, and is designed to respect mass and energy balances, monotone rheology, and momentum exchange with the ocean. We implement a diffusion-based architecture with conditional inputs for temperature, salinity, strain rate, and history, and embed physics-informed constraints through differentiable loss terms and a partial equation layer that enforces conservation. The surrogate yields ensembles of ice concentration, thickness, and ridging patterns at unresolved scales while remaining consistent with large-scale dynamics. We demonstrate substantial computational savings enabling real-time ensemble forecasting and efficient calibration, without sacrificing key statistics such as area coverage, compactness of ridges, and spectral characteristics of the ice field.

title: Simulating near-field enhancement in transmission of airborne viruses with a quadrature-based model.
text_ai: Some infectious diseases, such as influenza, tuberculosis, and SARS-CoV-2, may be transmitted when virus-laden particles expelled from an infectious person are inhaled by someone else, which is known as the airborne transmission route. These virus-laden particles are more concentrated in the expiratory jet of an infectious person than elsewhere in a well-mixed room, but this near-field enhancement in virion exposure has not been well quantified. Here, we develop a quadrature-based representation of near-field mixing that captures directional dependencies of expelled aerosols. The model partitions the exhaled jet into angular streams weighted by a quadrature scheme, enabling efficient estimation of local virion concentration in the near-field. Each stream is advected by a prescribed velocity field and interacts with a turbulence closure to approximate entrainment and dilution by ambient air. Particles are represented by a size-resolved concentration field, with virion load carried per particle and size-dependent settling and evaporation effects. We implement a two-way coupling between source strength and local concentration to reflect the transient nature of coughing and talking. Inactivation and deposition are included as first-order losses, while gravitational settling is included for larger aerosols. The model yields a set of one-dimensional transport equations along the chosen angular directions, solved simultaneously to reconstruct the full three-dimensional exposure field with reduced computational cost compared with full CFD. Validation is conducted against high-resolution CFD simulations of representative expiratory events and against experimental jet-plume measurements in a simplified chamber. The quadrature surrogate reproduces peak near-field concentrations within 10–20% for distances up to 0.8 m and captures angular decay of virion density. A parametric study demonstrates sensitivity of near-field exposure to source orientation, mouth opening, emission rate, particle size spectrum, and ventilation efficacy. Relative to a well-mixed-room assumption, near-field enhancement can contribute a substantial fraction of the cumulative inhaled dose during the initial seconds after emission, particularly for fine to mid-sized aerosols that remain airborne. Together, these results indicate that directional near-field transport modulates early infection risk and can be captured with modest computational cost. The quadrature-based surrogate provides a practical tool for rapid scenario screening and integration with occupancy and ventilation data to guide mitigation of short-range transmission.

title: An Optimal Algorithm for Computing the Spherical Depth of Points in the Plane
text_ai: For a distribution function $F$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$ and a point $q\in \mathbb{R}^d$, the \emph{spherical depth} $\SphD(q;F)$ is defined to be the probability that a point $q$ is contained inside a random closed hyper-ball obtained from a pair of points from $F$. The spherical depth $\SphD(q;S)$ is also defined for an arbitrary data set $S\subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ and $q\in \mathbb{R}^d$. Equivalently, q lies inside the closed ball with diameter XY iff the angle XQY is at least 90 degrees. In the plane this reduces SphD(q;S) to counting pairs {i,j} with vi = pi − q differing by at least π/2. We present an optimal O(n log n) time, O(n) space algorithm that computes this count exactly. Algorithm sketch: compute θi = atan2(yi − qy, xi − qx) for i, sort (θi,i), and extend by θi + 2π. For each i, Li is the first index with θ ≥ θi + π/2 and Ri the last with θ ≤ θi + 3π/2 in the extended array. Set ci = max(0, Ri − Li + 1). Ordered pairs total C = ∑i ci and unordered pairs total C/2. Then SphD(q;S) = (C/2) / (n choose 2). Endpoints included. We prove optimality in the comparison-based model: angular counting for SphD requires Ω(n log n) time, and our method attains this bound. Empirical results on synthetic data confirm substantial speedups over the naïve O(n^2) approach and robust performance as n or q vary.

The spherical depth $\SphD(q;S)$ is also defined for an arbitrary data set $S\subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ and $q\in \mathbb{R}^d$.

title: NuSTAR + XMM-Newton monitoring of the neutron star transient AX J1745.6-2901
text_ai: AX J1745.6-2901 is a high-inclination (eclipsing) transient neutron star (NS) Low Mass X-ray Binary (LMXB) showcasing intense ionised Fe K absorption. We present here the analysis of 11 XMM-Newton and 15 NuSTAR new data-sets (obtained between 2013-2016), therefore tripling the number of observations of AX J1745.6-2901 in outburst. Our joint XMM-Newton and NuSTAR campaign provides time-resolved, broadband spectroscopy (0.5–79 keV) across outbursts, enabling constraints on the flow and its ionized environment. The continuum is well described by a two-component model comprising a multicolor disk blackbody and a Comptonized boundary-layer emission, with a weak reflection component detected in several epochs. An ionized, blueshifted absorber is required in all observations, showing pronounced variability on timescales of days and clear dependence on orbital phase. Narrow Fe K features from Fe XXV and Fe XXVI are detected in most epochs with equivalent widths up to a few hundred eV. Photoionization modeling yields column densities NH,int ≈ 10^22.7–10^23.5 cm−2, ionization parameters log xi ≈ 3.2–3.8, and line-of-sight velocities up to ≈1500 km s−1, with higher ionization at higher luminosities. The absorber is often partially covering, consistent with a clumpy, equatorial disk wind intersecting the line of sight in this high-inclination system. We find an anti-correlation between line strength and ionization with luminosity; eclipse/dip phases constrain the wind geometry to lie near the orbital plane. Together, the results reveal a persistent disk wind in AX J1745.6-2901 and illustrate the efficacy of joint NuSTAR–XMM monitoring for wind studies in NS LMXBs.

title: A GPU-accelerated Large-scale Simulator for Transportation System Optimization Benchmarking
text_ai: With the development of artificial intelligence techniques, transportation system optimization is evolving from traditional methods relying on expert experience to simulation and learning-based decision and optimization methods. Learning-based optimization methods require extensive interactions with highly realistic microscopic traffic simulators. To address this demand, we present a GPU-accelerated large-scale simulator designed to generate and evaluate realistic traffic scenarios at metropolitan scales. The architecture integrates a discrete-event microscopic core with a highly parallel agent-based model, enabling the concurrent simulation of millions of vehicles with limited synchronization overhead. A novel parallelized car-following, lane-changing, and gap-acceptance module preserves emergent dynamics while exploiting data-parallel execution on modern GPUs. The simulation kernel runs on CUDA, with memory layouts organized to maximize coalesced accesses, while a lightweight host orchestrates scenario assembly, boundary conditions, and statistics collection. The framework supports complex networks, signal-controlled and adaptive intersections, dynamic demand generation, incident insertion, and heterogeneous vehicle fleets. We supply a benchmark harness for optimization tasks—route optimization, signal timing, and dynamic pricing—facilitating reproducible comparisons across learning-based and traditional approaches. A configurable evaluation protocol quantifies convergence, sample efficiency, and generalization across networks, along with system-level metrics such as travel-time distributions, queue length, emissions proxies, and energy consumption. Extensive experiments demonstrate near-linear GPU-speedups over optimized CPU baselines and strong scalability across network size and agent density. The distribution-wide benchmark suite enables fair benchmarking, protocol-validated results, and open reproducibility. To support reproducibility, the code and networks are released with detailed documentation.

title: Principles of Open Fracture Management
text_ai: Open fractures are contaminated wounds that contain gram-positive and gram-negative organisms; therefore, wide-spectrum antibiotic therapy should be incorporated into the treatment plan. Antibiotics should be initiated as soon after injury as possible, preferably within 3 hours of injury, after which time the rate of infection has been reported to increase. In parallel with antimicrobial therapy, definitive management hinges on prompt and meticulous debridement to remove all devitalized tissue, contaminated debris, and nonviable necrosis, preserving viable structures to the extent possible. The aim is to create a clean, well-vascularized wound bed capable of sustaining subsequent closure or coverage; debridement should be followed by thorough irrigation with isotonic saline. The role of adjunctive antiseptic or antibiotic irrigation remains controversial and should be individualized to wound characteristics and institutional protocols. Fracture stabilization should be achieved as soon as soft-tissue conditions permit; in extensive soft-tissue injury, temporary external fixation often affords wound access and tissue optimization, with definitive internal fixation deferred until coverage and edema have subsided and the risk of infection is minimized. In severe injuries (Gustilo-Anderson type III) or contaminated wounds with questionable tissue viability, early multidisciplinary planning for soft-tissue coverage is essential. Muscle or musculocutaneous flaps, regional flaps, or perforator-based reconstructions may be required to restore protective coverage and vascularity, typically coordinated with skeletal stabilization and performed within a window that balances infection risk against procedure-related morbidity. Negative-pressure wound therapy can serve as a bridge to definitive closure in selected cases, while definitive closure should be achieved through primary skin approximation when feasible, split-thickness grafts for smaller defects, or flap coverage for larger deficits. Postoperative management relies on serial wound assessments, vigilance for vascular or neural compromise, and adaptation of antimicrobial therapy guided by intraoperative cultures. Reassessment of fixation strategy is essential if soft-tissue healing lags or infection recurs. The principles outlined herein provide a framework for a staged, multidisciplinary approach that aims to minimize infection, promote healing, and preserve limb function across a spectrum of open fracture presentations.

title: Development and Validation of a Scale for Measuring Instructors' Attitudes toward Concept-Based or Reform-Oriented Teaching of Introductory Statistics in the Health and Behavioral Sciences
text_ai: Despite more than a decade of reform efforts, students continue to experience difficulty understanding and applying statistical concepts. The predominant focus of reform has been on content, pedagogy, technology and assessment, with little attention to instructor characteristics. However, there is strong theoretical and empirical evidence that instructors' attitudes impact the quality of teaching and learning. To address this gap, we undertook a multi-stage scale development workflow. Items were generated from the literature, instructor interviews, and expert reviews, yielding 32 candidate items. Pilot testing with 40 instructors and item analyses reduced this to 28 items. A large sample (N = 212) of health and behavioral sciences instructors completed the instrument and related indicators of teaching approach and demographics. Exploratory factor analysis supported a four-factor structure: Attitudes Toward Concept-Based/ Reform-Oriented Teaching (ATCR), Perceived Compatibility with Curricular Constraints (PCCC), Perceived Effectiveness and Outcomes (PEO), and Self-Efficacy for Implementing Reform (SEIR). Confirmatory factor analysis on a separate sample (N = 128) indicated good model fit (χ2/df ≈ 2.1; CFI ≈ .94; TLI ≈ .92; RMSEA ≈ .048). Reliability was high, with Cronbach's alpha values of .84–.92 for the subscales and .89 for the total scale. Construct validity evidence was established via correlations with teaching self-efficacy (r ≈ .57) and willingness to adopt reform-based practices (r ≈ .62), alongside modest discriminant validity from general attitudes toward statistics (r ≈ .20). These findings support the scale’s utility for diagnosing instructor predispositions, guiding professional development, and monitoring changes over time as reform initiatives unfold in health and behavioral sciences programs. Limitations include cross-sectional design and regional sampling; future work should test invariance across disciplines and languages and examine predictive validity for classroom practice and student outcomes.

title: Multi-dimensional band structure spectroscopy in the synthetic frequency dimension
text_ai: The concept of synthetic dimensions in photonics provides a versatile platform in exploring multi-dimensional physics. Many of these physics are characterized by band structures in more than one dimensions. Existing efforts on band structure measurements in the photonic synthetic frequency dimension however are limited to either one-dimensional Brillouin zones or one-dimensional subsets of multi-dimensional Brillouin zones. To overcome this limitation, we implement a two-dimensional spectroscopic protocol that resolves the complete band structure in the synthetic frequency space. Our platform comprises a chain of coupled ring resonators whose frequency ladder is shaped by phase-controlled modulation with two incommensurate tones, creating a two-dimensional lattice in (frequency, modulation index) space. By performing phase-sensitive, momentum-resolved excitation and recording the transmitted spectrum as the modulation phases are swept, we reconstruct ω(kx, ky) over a finite synthetic Brillouin zone. The reconstructed surfaces reveal conventional and topological features—band gaps, Dirac-type crossings, and edge-localized modes—and allow direct extraction of group velocities and Berry curvatures. The method is robust to moderate disorder and compatible with on-demand tuning of inter-dimensional couplings, enabling systematic exploration of multi-dimensional Floquet band physics.

title: Unraveling the emergence of quantum state designs in systems with symmetry
text_ai: Quantum state designs, by enabling an efficient sampling of random quantum states, play a quintessential role in devising and benchmarking various quantum protocols with broad applications ranging from circuit designs to black hole physics. Symmetries, on the other hand, are expected to reduce the randomness of a state. Here we show that the emergence of quantum state designs in the presence of symmetry is governed by representation-theoretic constraints that partition the Hilbert space into symmetry sectors. The t-th moment operator of a symmetry-preserving random circuit decomposes into a direct sum over irreps, so the global design property reduces to obtaining approximate t-designs within each sector with weights given by their dimensions. Employing Weingarten calculus adapted to block-diagonal ensembles and sector-wise concentration of measure, we derive bounds on the distance between the t-th moment of the symmetric circuit and that of the symmetric Haar measure. Our bounds reveal thresholds: approximate t-designs within a sector appear at circuit depths polynomial in n, t, and log(1/epsilon), while the overall depth is set by the smallest sector dimension, implying a potential slowdown set by the minimal irrep. We illustrate the framework with numerical simulations of spin chains endowed with U(1) and SU(2) symmetry, showing how charge and spin conservation modify scrambling and the approach to a state design. Crucially, for typical local symmetric circuits the design property is recovered across sectors at depths close to the unrestricted case up to polylogarithmic corrections in practice.

title: Gaps in treatment among users of osteoporosis medications: the dynamics of noncompliance
text_ai: PURPOSE: Cyclical patterns of compliance have been observed with many health-related activities such as dieting and exercise. It is not known whether such patterns of compliance exist among users of chronic medications. We sought to estimate the percentage of patients who restart osteoporosis therapy after a prolonged lapse in medication use and to identify the factors associated with a return to compliance. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using a large national health-plan claims database spanning 1995–2005. Included were adults aged ≥50 years who initiated anti-osteoporosis pharmacotherapy (oral bisphosphonates, denosumab, or zoledronic acid) with continuous enrollment for at least 12 months before initiation and at least 12 months thereafter. Discontinuation was defined as a gap ≥90 days without a refill after the expected end-date of the prior supply. A lapse was observed, and restart was defined as any subsequent prescription fill after lapse within 24 months. Time-to-restart was analyzed with Kaplan–Meier methods; Cox proportional hazards models identified predictors of restart, adjusting for demographics (age, sex, race/ethnicity), geographic region, Charlson comorbidity index, prior fracture, baseline osteoporosis-related claims, prior adherence (medication possession ratio), therapy type and duration before lapse, route of administration, and payer. RESULTS: Among 22,000 initiators, 7,100 experienced a lapse ≥90 days. Of these, 2,100 (30%) restarted within 12 months after lapse; the median time to restart was 7.8 months (IQR 5.0–12.3). By 24 months, 3,500 (50%) had restarted. In multivariable analysis, restart was more likely in women (HR 1.28, 95% CI 1.15–1.42), younger age (50–64 vs ≥75; HR 1.46, 95% CI 1.30–1.63), and higher prior adherence (MPR ≥0.8 vs <0.5; HR 2.05, 95% CI 1.84–2.29). Initiation with denosumab or intravenous zoledronic acid versus oral alendronate increased restart probability (HR 1.55, 95% CI 1.37–1.75). Higher comorbidity burden reduced restart likelihood (Charlson ≥3; HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.65–0.80). Longer lapse duration before restarting (per 30-day increment) decreased restart likelihood (HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.92–0.96). Regional access disparities attenuated after adjustment, though residual variation persisted. CONCLUSIONS: Gaps in osteoporosis therapy exhibit a measurable reinitiation fraction, but a substantial proportion does not resume treatment. Interventions at the time of lapse—such as patient education, streamlined reinitiation pathways, and consideration of regimens with less frequent dosing or immediate switching to parenteral therapy—may enhance long-term persistence and fracture risk reduction.

title: Early-life gut dysbiosis linked to juvenile mortality in ostriches.
text_ai: Imbalances in the gut microbial community (dysbiosis) of vertebrates have been associated with several gastrointestinal and autoimmune diseases. However, it is unclear which taxa are associated with gut dysbiosis, and if particular gut regions or specific time periods during ontogeny are more susceptible. To address these questions, we undertook a longitudinal multi-region microbiome survey of ostrich chicks (Struthio camelus) reared under commercial conditions. We sampled n=... individuals at hatch and days 7, 14, 28 and 56, obtaining luminal contents and mucosal scrapings from foregut (crop–proventriculus–gizzard), midgut (jejunum/ileum) and hindgut (caeca). DNA was subjected to V4 16S rRNA gene sequencing on Illumina MiSeq. Sequences were processed with DADA2 in QIIME2 to yield ASVs; taxonomy against SILVA 138. We assessed alpha diversity (Shannon, Faith's PD) and beta diversity (weighted/unweighted UniFrac) by region, timepoint and survival. ANCOM-BC identified differential abundance, with cage and maternal effects included as random factors. Functional potential was inferred with PICRUSt2. Results reveal an early-life disturbance by day 7, dominated by Proteobacteria (Enterobacterales) and depleted Lachnospiraceae/Ruminococcaceae. The dysbiosis was most pronounced in hindgut mucosa and persisted through day 28 in chicks that subsequently died. Survivors maintained higher proportions of Bacteroidota and Firmicutes, with a stable cohort of butyrate producers. Beta diversity trajectories separated mortalities from survivors (PERMANOVA, P<0.001); time-to-event analyses linked early hindgut dysbiosis to mortality risk (hazard ratios 2–3 per SD). Predicted functions suggested increased endotoxin biosynthesis and reduced saccharolytic capacity in dysbiotic samples. Conclusions: Early-life gut dysbiosis is associated with juvenile mortality in ostriches, with region-specific signatures and lasting functional consequences. Interventions during hatch and early rearing that promote colonization by beneficial fermenters or dampen proteobacterial blooms may reduce mortality risk. The findings offer a framework for biomarker-driven monitoring and microbiome-stabilization strategies in juvenile ostriches.

title: Using Spectral Radius Ratio for Node Degree to Analyze the Evolution of Scale Free Networks and Small World Networks
text_ai: In this paper, we show the evaluation of the spectral radius for node degree as the basis to analyze the variation in the node degrees during the evolution of scale-free networks and small-world networks. Employing a time-resolved SRR metric, we quantify how the degree-driven spectral radius evolves under growth mechanisms. The study introduces an operational definition of the spectral radius ratio, computed from the adjacency-derived degree operator and benchmarked against Erdős–Rényi and configuration-model null models. We analyze synthetic networks generated by the Barabási–Albert preferential attachment process and by the Watts–Strogatz rewiring scheme across a range of sizes (N) and mean degrees ⟨k⟩, together with real-world networks. Our results show that SRR tracks the emergence of hub dominance in scale-free growth, displaying a characteristic ascent that correlates with tail exponent and the accrual of high-degree nodes. Conversely, in small-world regimes, SRR stabilizes around a baseline with small fluctuations governed by clustering and shortcuts. The metric demonstrates predictive utility for transition points and offers a compact descriptor for evolutionary stage, enabling early discrimination of topology formation pathways.

title: HYPE: Hyperbolic Entailment Filtering for Underspecified Images and Texts
text_ai: In an era where the volume of data drives the effectiveness of self-supervised learning, the specificity and clarity of data semantics play a crucial role in model training. Addressing this, we introduce HYPerbolic Entailment filtering (HYPE), a novel methodology designed to meticulously extract modality-wise meaningful and well-aligned data from extensive, noisy image-text pair datasets. Specifically, HYPE encodes cross-modal relationships in a hyperbolic geometry, where hierarchy mirrors entailment strength and content specificity. We compute an entailment score by projecting image regions and textual predicates into a shared Poincaré ball, extracting distance-based confidence bounds that penalize underconstrained descriptions. The filtering pipeline combines candidate-pair mining with a calibrated cross-modal entailment classifier trained on curated supervision and reinforced by a hyperbolic regularizer that preserves hierarchy. Pairs passing a defined threshold compose a high-fidelity training corpus, while ambiguous instances are quarantined or re-annotated. Applying HYPE to standard vision-language benchmarks yields cleaner supervision, improved retrieval precision, and stronger zero-shot generalization. Ablation confirms the advantage of hyperbolic geometry over Euclidean baselines, particularly in spaces with nested semantic structures and underspecified captions, in practice.

title: Tribute to Henry Primakoff: Chiral Perturbation Theory Tests via Primakoff Reactions
text_ai: Consider the scattering of GeV energy beam particles off the Coulomb field of a nucleus. In this context, the Coulomb field behaves like a target of $\gamma^*$ virtual photons, with the target density being proportional to Z$^2$. Henry Primakoff was the first to describe how to determine the $\pi^0$ lifetime by measuring the production cross section for the process $\gamma\gamma^* \rightarrow \pi^0$. Building on Primakoff's insight, the forward differential cross section is analyzed to isolate the electromagnetic Primakoff amplitude, shaped by the nuclear form factor and coherence length. Using high‑Z targets and Energetic beams, the γγ* → P (P=π^0, η, η') transition form factors are extracted in a regime where hadronic backgrounds are suppressed and the anomaly-driven width Γ(P→γγ) can be confronted with ChPT predictions. The analysis juxtaposes contemporary ChPT calculations, including higher‑order loops and resonance–saturation inputs, with dispersive and lattice determinations of the relevant low‑energy constants. We discuss experimental strategies to control backgrounds, radiative corrections, and nuclear screening, outlining how upcoming Primakoff programs will sharpen tests of the chiral anomaly and the structure of the pseudoscalar sector.

title: An exact relation between number of black box computations required to solve an oracle problem quantumly and quantum retrocausality
text_ai: We investigate the reason for the quantum speedup -- quantum algorithms requiring fewer computation steps than their classical counterparts. We extend their representation to the process of setting the problem. The initial measurement selects a setting at random, Bob (the problem setter) unitarily changes it into the desired one. We adopt a time-symmetric, two-boundary representation in which the computation is described by a pair of boundary conditions: the initial random setting imposed by Bob and a postselected final measurement outcome that signals algorithmic success. In this framework, part of the information determining the problem's instance is supplied at preparation, whereas part is effectively supplied retrocausally by the selection at the end. We quantify this retrocausal contribution by a boundary-information measure R, defined as the maximal increase in success probability achievable by conditioning on the final outcome beyond the forwardly supplied setting. We then show that, for any oracle problem with a fixed success probability, the minimal number of oracle uses Q_q in the quantum setting satisfies an exact identity with the classical lower bound Q_c: Q_q = Q_c − R, where 0 ≤ R ≤ Q_c and R attains its maximum only if the final measurement perfectly retroinforms the problem setting. The equality holds under unitary oracle operations and projective measurements within the boundary constraints. We illustrate the principle by analyzing canonical problems (Deutsch–Jozsa, Simon's, and unstructured search) and by constructing explicit two-boundary protocols that realize the bound without violating causality or no-signalling. The demonstrated relation clarifies why quantum speedups emerge as a redistribution of information between preparation and postselection, within a time-symmetric account. The results bear on the interpretation of quantum computation, the role of measurement in algorithmic efficiency, and potential experimental probes of retrocausal computational strategies.

title: AI-Based Multi-Object Relative State Estimation with Self-Calibration Capabilities
text_ai: The capability to extract task specific, semantic information from raw sensory data is a crucial requirement for many applications of mobile robotics. Autonomous inspection of critical infrastructure with Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), for example, requires precise navigation relative to the structure that is to be inspected. In this work, we present an AI-based framework for multi-object relative state estimation with online self-calibration of sensor extrinsics, tailored to autonomous infrastructure inspection using UAVs. The system jointly reasons about the relative poses between the vehicle and multiple scene targets (e.g., structural features, joints, plaques) while continuously refining the camera–IMU extrinsics despite sensor drift. A modular perception front end delivers robust detections and cross-view correspondences, which feed a probabilistic tracker and a sliding-window optimizer that enforces geometric consistency across objects and time. Learned factors encode semantic affinities and correspondence uncertainty, while a self-calibration loop updates calibration parameters online without manual intervention. Evaluation on real-world UAV campaigns and simulated scenarios demonstrates improved robustness to occlusion and viewpoint change, with accurate relative state estimates and stable calibration across flights.

title: Tidal evolution and diffusive growth during high-eccentricity planet migration: revisiting the eccentricity distribution of hot Jupiters
text_ai: High-eccentricity tidal migration is a potential formation channel for hot Jupiters. During this process, the planetary f-mode may experience a phase of diffusive growth, allowing its energy to quickly build up to large values. In Yu et al. , the stochastic growth of the planetary f-mode was shown to initiate diffusive energy buildup capable of rapid orbital decay during high-eccentricity encounters. Here we extend that framework by including nonlinear mode coupling, energy leakage into the planet, and a self-consistent orbital–mode treatment. We develop a hybrid approach evolving E_f on periastron passages with a diffusion term D(E_f) and a drift from tidal dissipation, updating orbital elements when E_f crosses a dissipation threshold. A damping term Γ_f accounts for wave leakage and internal damping. We perform Monte Carlo synthesis across initial masses 0.5–3 M_J, initial semi-major axes 0.2–1.5 AU, and initial eccentricities 0.3–0.95 around solar-type hosts. Across the ensemble, diffusive growth broadens the locus of configurations yielding hot Jupiters and shortens migration times for many cases. The eccentricity distribution at circularization is more populated at modest e (∼0.1–0.3) than in deterministic-tide models, with a suppressed tail at e > 0.5 unless damping is weak. Integrated over representative stellar populations, the predicted hot-Jupiter frequency aligns with observational estimates for plausible diffusion coefficients and saturation. Our results show diffusive f-mode growth is a viable contributor to hot-Jupiter demographics and provides a framework to interpret the observed eccentricity distribution in high-e migration scenarios.

title: The heptad repeat domain 1 of Mitofusin has membrane destabilization function in mitochondrial fusion.
text_ai: Mitochondria are double-membrane-bound organelles that constantly change shape through membrane fusion and fission. Outer mitochondrial membrane fusion is controlled by Mitofusin, whose molecular architecture consists of an N-terminal GTPase domain, a first heptad repeat domain (HR1), two transmembrane domains, and a second heptad repeat domain (HR2). Here, we test the mechanistic contribution of HR1 to outer-membrane fusion by combining in vitro reconstitution with cellular assays. Purified HR1 and HR1-containing fragments reconstituted with liposomes induce dose-dependent leakage of encapsulated dye and enhanced lipid mixing, indicating bilayer destabilization compatible with fusion intermediates. Biophysical analyses identify an amphipathic helix in HR1 whose hydrophobic face engages lipid acyl chains, with a preference for cardiolipin-rich membranes. Mutational disruption of conserved hydrophobic residues abrogates leakage and fusion, establishing causality. In proteoliposome assays, HR1 cooperates with HR2 to accelerate content release, whereas HR1 alone cannot complete pore formation. In cells, mitofusin variants lacking functional HR1 impede outer-membrane tethering–fusion efficiency. Our results define HR1 as a membrane-destabilizing module that lowers the energy barrier to fusion and that is modulated by the GTPase-driven conformational cycle.

title: International clinical practice recommendations on the definition, diagnosis, assessment, intervention, and psychosocial aspects of developmental coordination disorder.
text_ai: These international clinical practice recommendations (CPR) for developmental coordination disorder (DCD), initiated by the European Academy of Childhood Disability (EACD), aim to address key questions on the definition, diagnosis, assessment, intervention, and psychosocial aspects of DCD relevant for clinical practice. Key questions in five areas were considered through literature reviews and formal expert consensus. The CPR provides evidence-informed recommendations across five domains—definition and diagnostic criteria, assessment, intervention, and psychosocial aspects—with applicability across pediatric, adolescent, and school-based services and across diverse health-care systems. A harmonized definition for DCD is reaffirmed: motor coordination substantially below age- and opportunity-expected levels, resulting in difficulties in activities of daily living and educational participation, with onset in early development, and not better explained by intellectual disability, visual impairment, or a known neurological/medical condition. Diagnostic work should integrate standardized motor assessments with clinical judgment, account for comorbidity and functional impact, and employ a staged, multi-informant approach that includes developmental history, observations of performance in familiar tasks, and ecological evaluation of participation and disability. In the assessment domain, the recommendations advocate use of validated, age-appropriate motor measures (e.g., standardized tests with normative data) complemented by observations of movement quality, performance in real-world tasks, and participation indices. Clinicians should rule out alternative etiologies, screen for co-occurring conditions (e.g., ADHD, learning disorders, sensory processing differences), and document baseline functioning and goals. Information from families, educators, and other professionals is essential, as is ongoing monitoring of progress and responsiveness to intervention across settings and over time. Interventions should be multimodal, individualized, and contextually embedded, combining skill-focused practice with person- and task-specific strategies, environmental adaptations, and supports within home, school, and community environments. The recommendations emphasize collaborative goal setting, dose and progression tailored to needs and resources, caregiver and educator coaching, and adherence to principles of inclusive, participation-oriented rehabilitation. Consideration of accessibility, equity, and cultural relevance across settings is urged. Psychosocial aspects are prioritized through routine screening for self-esteem, anxiety, social participation, and mental health concerns, with emphasis on family-centered care, stigma reduction, peer inclusion, and transition planning. The CPR also outlines implementation guidance, dissemination resources, and research priorities to improve uptake and outcomes, while acknowledging gaps and the need for ongoing refinement across populations.

title: Computational analysis of flow structures in turbulent ventricular blood flow associated with mitral valve intervention
text_ai: Cardiac disease and clinical intervention may both lead to an increased risk for thrombosis events due to modified blood flow in the heart, and thereby a change in the mechanical stimuli of blood cells passing through the chambers of the heart. To quantify these effects, we constructed patient-specific left ventricular models incorporating mitral valve device geometries derived from pre- and post-intervention imaging. Transient, 3D CFD simulations were performed on deforming LV cavities to reproduce diastolic filling and systolic ejection across cardiac cycles, with boundary conditions imposed by measured inflow and outflow waveforms and three-element Windkessel models. The mitral orifice and prosthetic components were represented explicitly to capture jet–wall interactions and potential obstruction. End-diastolic meshes were aligned with cine MRI data to preserve realistic wall motion; wall motion was prescribed or coupled via a reduced-fluid-structure approach to reflect compliance changes after intervention. We resolved turbulent structures with a hybrid approach: RANS in the bulk with localized LES near the jet and the prosthesis to resolve high-shear features, enabling accurate computation of vorticity, energy spectra, and time-dependent shear metrics. Flow topology was analyzed using Q-criterion and lambda-2 isosurfaces to identify coherent vortical structures, while Lagrangian methods (FTLE fields and particle tracking) defined transport barriers and residence times. Thrombogenic potential was quantified with a platelet activation index combining shear exposure and dwell time in high-shear domains. Results show that mitral intervention alters diastolic jet morphology and intraventricular mixing, reducing sustained mid-ventricular recirculation in most cases but introducing localized high-shear jets tethered to device surfaces. Consequently, global turbulent kinetic energy decreased modestly while peak localized shear rose transiently near prosthetic interfaces. Across patients, changes in oscillatory shear and residence-time distributions correlated with projected reductions in a global platelet-activation metric, though regions adjacent to devices remained at elevated risk in a subset. The framework thus links device-induced flow topology to thrombogenic potential and offers a quantitative tool to guide device design and patient-specific planning.

title: Energy Gap from Step Structure of the Analytically Inverted Non-Additive Kinetic Potential
text_ai: The bandgap constitutes a challenging problem in density functional theory (DFT) methodologies. It is known that the energy gap values calculated by common DFT approaches are underestimated. The bandgap was also found to be related to the derivative discontinuity (DD) of the exchange-correlation potential in the Kohn-Sham formulation of DFT. Here we analyze step structure of analytically inverted non-additive kinetic potential (NAKP) for fragments forming a molecular or extended system. We show that the interfacial step in the NAKP reflects the derivative discontinuity (DD) of the exact exchange–correlation potential and that its height equals the DD shared between fragments. Consequently the fundamental gap, defined as the difference between vertical ionization potential and electron affinity, can be decomposed as the Kohn–Sham gap plus the DD recovered from the NAKP step. We derive an inversion workflow that yields the NAKP and its steps directly from density, without recourse to many-body perturbation theory. The approach is tested on benchmarks—small diatomics, charge-transfer complexes, and organic semiconductors—where the exact DD is known or closely approximated. Gaps obtained from the inverted NAKP step match experimental gaps and high level theories with accuracy, and they display sensitivity to environmental and subsystem coupling. Importantly, the method remains stable across fractional occupations and provides insight into how embedding-induced steps govern gap formation in non-additive kinetic frameworks. Our findings establish the step of analytically inverted NAKP as a diagnostic and predictive handle for energy gap in DFT embedding.

title: Neuropeptidase activity in the frontal cortex of Wistar-Kyoto and spontaneously hypertensive rats treated with vasoactive drugs: a bilateral study.
text_ai: Hypertension can lead to mood disorders that may worsen or ameliorate depending on the type of antihypertensive prescribed. Depression is associated with modifications in basal brain asymmetry particularly that of the frontal cortex, which is involved in blood pressure control. Furthermore, different vasoactive drugs may change the brain's asymmetry in a manner that contributes to cognition status. Here, we evaluated basal and pharmacologically modulated bilateral neuropeptidase activity in the frontal cortex of WKY and SHR rats exposed to three clinically relevant vasoactive compounds (captopril, hydralazine, and prazosin). Enzymatic hydrolysis of substrate analogs for representative neuropeptidases implicated in peptidergic signaling was measured in left and right frontal cortices, enabling assessment of hemispheric asymmetries and their modulation by hypertensive status and drug exposure. Experimental groups included vehicle controls and drug-treated cohorts, with analyses conducted after a defined treatment period to capture both acute and subacute effects on enzymatic activity. Assays were performed under standardized conditions, and activity was expressed relative to protein content to permit cross-comparison between hemispheres and strains. Baseline asymmetry differed between strains, with SHR exhibiting a tendency toward greater rightward or leftward deviation in selected peptidase activities compared with WKY, a pattern that paralleled known alterations in frontal cortical function associated with hypertension. Drug treatments produced genotype-specific alterations in neuropeptidase activity, frequently revealing bidirectional shifts that reshaped the bilateral activity profile. Captopril tended to dampen hyperactive peptidase pathways in SHR, reducing interhemispheric discrepancies, whereas hydralazine favored a more symmetric but strain-dependent modulation. Prazosin elicited lateralized changes, most evident in WKY, where left-right differences shifted in a direction consistent with altered peptidergic tone in circuitry implicated in autonomic and affective regulation. Across strains, the magnitude and direction of drug-induced changes correlated with cardiovascular status and, in some cases, with behavioral correlates reported in parallel experiments, suggesting a link between vascular pharmacotherapy, frontal cortex neuropeptidase activity, and hemispheric asymmetry. In sum, the data indicate that neuropeptidase activity in the frontal cortex is modulated by hypertensive phenotype and vasoactive drugs in a bilateral, drug- and strain-dependent manner, with potential implications for mood-cognition–vascular interactions.
