title: Nonconservation of lepton current and asymmetry of relic neutrinos
text_ai: The neutrino asymmetry in the early universe plasma, $n_\nu - n_{\bar \nu}$, is calculated both before and after the electroweak phase transition (EWPT). The leptogenesis before EWPT within the standard model is well known to be driven by the abelian anomaly in a massless hypercharge field. Beyond the standard pre-EWPT leptogenesis, we formulate the evolution of the lepton-number current from anomaly-induced source terms in a magnetized primordial plasma. The key equation is ∂μ j_L^μ = -(g'^2/16π^2) Y^{μν} \tilde{Y}_{μν}, linking the time variation of the net lepton number to the helicity and energy density of hypermagnetic fields. We employ a mean-field treatment of the hypercharge sector, allowing for a helical field with finite conductivity σ, and we include chirality-flipping processes driven by Yukawa interactions that become efficient as the EWPT is approached. The numerics integrate the coupled system for nν − nνbar and the hypermagnetic helicity H_Y, with seed fields compatible with causal magnetogenesis scenarios. We then follow the transfer across the electroweak crossover, where hypercharge polarization partly converts into electromagnetic helicity, modifying the lepton current through the same anomaly term. Below the EWPT, the anomaly is effectively replaced by the QED counterpart and by sphaleron dynamics that continue to couple to B+L violation and to the lepton numbers. The resulting relic neutrino asymmetry is presented as Δν ≡ nν − nνbar after decoupling, and its magnitude is confronted with bounds from BBN and CMB on the neutrino chemical potentials. Within plausible hypermagnetic-field configurations, we identify regions of parameter space where the asymmetry remains finite after dilution and is compatible with observational limits, thereby establishing a viable link between nonconservation of the lepton current in the early plasma, primordial magnetogenesis, and the relic neutrino sector.

title: A Dynamic Data Structure for Representing Timed Transitive Closures on Disk
text_ai: Temporal graphs represent interactions between entities over time. These interactions may be direct, a contact between two vertices at some time instant, or indirect, through sequences of contacts called journeys. Deciding whether an entity can reach another through a journey is useful for various applications in complex networks. We present a dynamic external‑memory data structure that maintains the timed transitive closure (TTC) of a temporal graph under insertion and deletion of contacts. The TTC encodes, for every pair of vertices, whether a time‑respecting journey exists within a horizon; the information is persisted on disk in a time‑annotated reachability index and queried with I/O cost. The core idea is a hierarchical time decomposition that partitions time into a logarithmic number of levels and stores per‑vertex forward and backward reachability summaries at each level. A lightweight delta log records updates and is consulted to answer queries against the current state without full rebuilds. Query processing merges base TTC blocks with pending deltas: a reachability query (s,t,τ) is satisfied if there exists a forward path from s to t via edges with times ≤ τ, as captured by the level summaries. Updates propagate only along the affected frontier; we employ lazy propagation and batched recompression of temporal arborescences to bound I/O. We prove correctness and obtain amortized I/O bounds in the external‑memory model. Empirical evaluation on synthetic and real temporal networks shows that the structure scales to graphs with millions of contacts, delivering query latency close to in‑memory baselines while reducing update cost by factors of several × compared to recomputation. The approach is amenable to concurrent access and streaming workloads, and the compact index enables practical deployment on commodity hardware.

title: Towards Practical Implementations of Person Re-Identification from Full Video Frames
text_ai: With the major adoption of automation for cities security, person re-identification (Re-ID) has been extensively studied recently. In this paper, we argue that the current way of studying person re-identification, i.e. by trying to re-identify a person within already detected and pre-cropped images of people, is not sufficient to implement practical security applications, where the inputs to the system are the full frames of the video streams. To this end, we present a unified pipeline that performs person detection, tracking and re-identification directly from full frames. The core contribution is a joint optimization that learns frame-level representations while enforcing temporal consistency across detections belonging to the same individual. We propose a temporal attention and memory module that aggregates features along tracklets, mitigating occlusions and abrupt pose changes. A contextual background suppression component reduces distractors by modeling scene content and camera geometry. The system is designed for practical deployment with real-time throughput on commodity GPUs and low annotation demand through self-supervised pretraining on unlabeled video streams. We benchmark the framework on extended video-re-id collections capturing continuous camera flows, reporting end-to-end identification accuracy, track purity, and end-to-end latency as primary operational metrics for real-world validation and deployment.

title: HEX: Hierarchical Emergence Exploitation in Self-Supervised Algorithms
text_ai: In this paper, we propose an algorithm that can be used on top of a wide variety of self-supervised (SSL) approaches to take advantage of hierarchical structures that emerge during training. SSL approaches typically work through some invariance term to ensure consistency between similar samples and a regularization term to prevent global dimensional collapse. HEX achieves this by introducing a lightweight, plug-in module that constructs a hierarchy of pseudo-views from SSL representations, requiring no additional labels or architectural changes to the backbone. At regular intervals during training, HEX builds a multi-scale partition of the current representation space, yielding levels of granularity from coarse to fine. Each level supplies a set of pseudo-labels that define level-specific contrastive objectives. The core objective aggregates across levels with learnable weights and includes a cross-level consistency term to stabilize cluster assignments across training, thereby mitigating level drift. A gating mechanism dynamically selects, for each instance, the most informative level to enforce at a given step, enabling adaptive exploitation of emergent structure. To support stable learning, HEX maintains a memory bank of level-specific prototypes and employs efficient in-batch and prototype-based negative sampling. The resulting HEX objective can be plugged into a wide range of SSL backbones—contrastive, predictive, or clustering-based—incurring only modest computational overhead and no extra data requirements. We evaluate HEX on standard vision benchmarks, integrating with multiple SSL baselines, and observe consistent improvements in linear evaluation accuracy and downstream transfer performance, including segmentation- and detection-oriented tasks. Ablation studies verify the necessity of hierarchical discovery, cross-level regularization, and the gating decision. Theoretical analysis characterizes HEX as a hierarchy-aware regularizer that aligns emergent representation geometry with multi-scale discriminability, thereby enabling more faithful capture of data structure without supervision. Overall, HEX provides a general, scalable mechanism to harness hierarchical emergence in self-supervised learning.

title: The H - Omega_o Diagram From Recent CMB Observations: Yes, We Can Already Say Something
text_ai: The CMB is already one of the pillars of the Big Bang model. However it may also become our most powerful tool to distinguish contending models and to determine their cosmological parameters. To realize this goal, more than 20 observational groups and two new satellites are gearing up to make precise measurements of the CMB at small angular scales. Here we present a concise synthesis of how the most recent small-scale measurements of the CMB translate into a direct H0–Ω0 diagram, and what this implies for the standard cosmological model and its minimal extensions. We jointly analyze TT, TE, EE, and lensing power spectra from Planck, the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) and the South Pole Telescope (SPT), using skyline priors on calibration, beam, and foreground residuals constrained by multi-frequency data. The angular positions of the acoustic peaks fix θ*, which translates into a curved degeneracy between H0 and Ω0 that is nearly orthogonal to the line of constant matter density today, enabling a precise determination of the allowed region. Our results show that, under a ΛCDM assumption with negligible curvature, the data prefer H0 in the 66–68 km s−1 Mpc−1 range and Ω0 very close to unity, with marginalized uncertainties at the few percent level. Allowing modest curvature (|Ωk| ≲ 0.01) or mild deviations from w = −1 broadens the contour but preserves the overall consistency, disfavoring markedly non-flat geometries or exotic energy components at high significance. Foreground and instrumental systematics are shown not to erase the core inference; the H–Ω0 diagram remains a robust discriminator between competing cosmologies, even with current data alone.

title: Magnetically-driven explosions of rapidly-rotating white dwarfs following Accretion-Induced Collapse
text_ai: We present 2D multi-group flux-limited diffusion magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) simulations of the Accretion-Induced Collapse (AIC) of a rapidly-rotating white dwarf. We focus on the dynamical role of MHD processes after the formation of a millisecond-period protoneutron star. Across a parameter space with initial spin periods near breakup and dipolar poloidal field strengths of 10^9–10^10 G, the simulations follow the collapse to a millisecond protoneutron star. Differential rotation rapidly winds the field, amplifying the toroidal component by factors of tens to hundreds within ≲ 50 ms and driving magnetic stresses that exceed gas pressure in the inner tens of kilometers. A magnetically dominated funnel forms along the rotation axis, producing a bipolar outflow whose acceleration and collimation are controlled by the evolving field geometry. The magnetic tower extracts angular momentum from the proto-neutron star and transfers momentum to the surrounding mantle, unbinding a substantial fraction of the inner envelope. The ejecta masses are in the ∼0.01–0.1 Msun range with kinetic energies of a few 10^50 erg and asymptotic speeds up to (1–2)×10^4 km s^−1. Neutrino heating, included via 3-group flux-limited diffusion, provides a modest early push but remains subdominant relative to magnetic acceleration at later times. AIC-formed explosions thus appear magnetically driven for rapidly rotating progenitors, with a robust, albeit axisymmetric, jet-like morphology and significant anisotropy. The results are relatively insensitive to moderate variations in initial field topology, though pure poloidal fields yield weaker, less-collimated outflows. We discuss implications for transient phenomenology, nucleosynthetic yields, and multi-messenger signatures, and outline how 3D effects will modify collimation and saturation of the magnetic fields, refining predictions for observational diagnostics.

title: On exponentiality of automorphisms of ${\bf A}^n$ of order $p$ in characteristic $p>0$
text_ai: Let $X$ be an integral affine scheme of characteristic $p>0$, and $\sigma $ a non-identity automorphism of $X$. If $\sigma $ is $\textit{exponential}$, i.e., induced from a ${\bf G}_a$-action on $X$, then $\sigma $ is obviously of order $p$. It is easy to see that the converse is not true in general. Let k be a field of characteristic p>0 and X=A^n_k. We give a complete characterization of exponential automorphisms of order p in Aut_k(X). We prove that σ has order p and is exponential iff σ arises from a Ga-action Ga × X → X; equivalently, there exists a nontrivial locally nilpotent p-derivation D together with an associated iterative higher-derivation for which σ is the truncated exponential. In particular the linear part of σ is unipotent and satisfies (I+N)^p=I, N^p=0. The main tool is the Hasse–Schmidt theory of p-derivations and their integration to Ga-actions in positive characteristic. As consequences we obtain normal forms up to Aut_k(X)-conjugacy in low dimension (n≤3), and obstructions to exponentiality in higher dimensions via standard invariants (e.g., Makar-Limanov). We also present explicit families illustrating the dichotomy between exponential and non-exponential order-p automorphisms in characteristic p>0.

title: Simultaneous Segmentation and Recognition: Towards more accurate Ego Gesture Recognition
text_ai: Ego hand gestures can be used as an interface in AR and VR environments. While the context of an image is important for tasks like scene understanding, object recognition, image caption generation and activity recognition, it plays a minimal role in ego hand gesture recognition. Here, we propose a unified framework that jointly performs hand segmentation and gesture recognition in ego-centric streams, exploiting the complementary information between spatial masks and gesture semantics. The architecture comprises a shared feature extractor, a segmentation decoder predicting a per-pixel hand mask, and a recognition head that outputs gesture probabilities. A temporal module aggregates features across a short temporal window. A cross-task attention mechanism allows segmentation to inform recognition by emphasizing foreground pixels, while recognition signals refine segmentation by constraining masks to gesture-relevant regions. Training minimizes a multi-task loss: a standard segmentation objective (Dice/BCE), a recognition cross-entropy with label smoothing, and a consistency term aligning mask quality with recognition reliability, and temporal regularization. We demonstrate that joint optimization yields more accurate masks and more robust gesture predictions under variable backgrounds and occlusions, compared to two-stage pipelines. Ablation confirms the contribution of segmentation guidance, temporal modeling and cross-task attention, with qualitative results illustrating improved boundary fidelity.

title: Funding pharmacists in general practice: A feasibility study to inform the design of future economic evaluations.
text_ai: Funding is a significant barrier to employing general practice pharmacists. To explore the feasibility of determining the cost-benefit of pharmacists in Australian general practice. Two part-time pharmacists were employed by general practices in Canberra, Australia. Diaries of the pharmacists were analysed to determine time worked and participation in income-generating activities, including Government-funded programs: Asthma Cycle of Care, Home Medicine Reviews, and Health Care Assessments. Diary data were triangulated with practice records and semi-structured interviews to validate time estimates and identify barriers to engagement with income-generating activities. A simple cost model compared gross revenue attributable to each program with pharmacist labour costs, practice overhead, and program-specific remuneration rules. Findings suggest that pharmacists allocated most time to patient-facing activities, particularly Home Medicine Reviews and Health Care Assessments, with substantial inter-practice variation. Administrative and coordination duties consumed non-trivial portions of schedules, attenuating net income. When non-financial benefits were included qualitatively—such as improvements in medication safety and patient satisfaction—the perceived value increased, though standardised economic valuation proved infeasible within the pilot period. Feasibility of diary-based time capture and basic costing was demonstrated, informing design considerations for future randomised or controlled economic evaluations, including required sample sizes, data collection cadence, and outcomes to monetise.

title: CorrectNav: Self-Correction Flywheel Empowers Vision-Language-Action Navigation Model
text_ai: Existing vision-and-language navigation models often deviate from the correct trajectory when executing instructions. However, these models lack effective error correction capability, hindering their recovery from errors. To address this challenge, we propose Self-correction Flywheel, a novel post-training paradigm. Self-correction Flywheel integrates three modules: an error detector, a correction generator, and a policy updater. During post-training, the model executes varied instructions in a controlled environment; an external critic flags trajectory deviations and yields corrective signals. The correction generator proposes plausible remedies conditioned on current state, visual input, and instruction semantics. The flywheel updates the base vision-language-action navigator with small, stabilizing corrections via imitation learning and off-policy fine-tuning, preserving capabilities while improving recovery. To scale, we collect perturbed trajectories and simulated fallbacks, and apply a curriculum that gradually increases failure modes. We evaluate on standard VLN benchmarks (R2R, CVDN) under perception and language noise. Our method yields higher success rates and shorter path lengths with modest inference overhead. Ablation shows the error-feedback loop and the correction generator drive most gains, while post-training cost remains reasonable. Overall, CorrectNav enables autonomous recovery from missteps, reducing cumulative deviation and boosting reliability in instruction-following navigation.

title: Routing Protocols Performance in Mobile Ad-Hoc Networks Using Millimeter Wave
text_ai: Self-Organized networks (SONs) have been studied for many years, and have attracted many researchers due to their substantial applications. Although the performance of such networks in the lower band networks (sub-6 GHz band frequencies) has been well studied, there are only sparse studies on SON in higher frequency bands, such as the millimeter wave (mmWave) band ranges between 28GHz and 300GHz. To this end, we evaluate the performance of routing protocols under a mmWave-powered mobile ad-hoc network. We model directional transmissions with realistic blockage, path loss, and beam-alignment overhead. Three paradigms—on-demand (AODV), source-route (DSR), and proactive (OLSR)—are implemented atop a mmWave PHY/MAC stack and tested across node densities (20–100), speeds (0–20 m/s), traffic loads, and mobility patterns. Key metrics include packet delivery ratio, end-to-end latency, throughput, routing overhead, and energy consumption. Results show that mmWave enhances per-link capacity but introduces severe directional alignment costs and frequent link outages under mobility, leading to degraded PDR and latency for reactive protocols when beam training dominates. Incorporating a link-stability metric and adaptive beamwidth in routing decisions yields noticeable gains. The results provide guidelines for routing protocol selection and cross-layer optimization in mmWave MANETs in practice.

title: Domain-knowledge Inspired Pseudo Supervision (DIPS) for Unsupervised Image-to-Image Translation Models to Support Cross-Domain Classification
text_ai: The ability to classify images is dependent on having access to large labeled datasets and testing on data from the same domain that the model can train on. Classification becomes more challenging when dealing with new data from a different domain, where gathering and especially labeling a larger image dataset for retraining a classification model requires a labor-intensive human effort. To address this, we propose Domain-knowledge Inspired Pseudo Supervision (DIPS), a framework that injects task- and domain-grounded cues into unsupervised image-to-image translation to support cross-domain classification without target-domain labels. DIPS leverages domain knowledge—semantic hierarchies, invariances, and class priors—to generate pseudo-supervision signals that steer translations toward semantic consistency. The approach couples a cycle-consistent translator with a pseudo-supervision branch that distills source-domain features for the target task, while a student classifier learns on translated samples. We decompose the objective into three components: (i) a translation fidelity term preserving structure, (ii) a pseudo-label alignment term that transfers source-domain opinions via cross-domain consistency, and (iii) a domain-regularization term encoding domain relationships and invariances. We validate DIPS on cross-domain benchmarks spanning synthetic-to-real and weather-variant imagery. Against leading unsupervised domain adaptation and UI2I baselines, DIPS yields higher target-domain accuracy with little or no target labels. Ablations isolate the impact of each pseudo-supervision signal and the amount of domain knowledge. Across tasks, the approach yields more robust, semantically consistent translations and improved cross-domain classification with reduced labeling effort. The framework remains compatible with limited target-domain labeling when available, offering an additive boost in performance across diverse visual domains.

title: An Effective Crop-Paste Pipeline for Few-shot Object Detection
text_ai: Few-shot object detection (FSOD) aims to expand an object detector for novel categories given only a few instances for training. However, detecting novel categories with only a few samples usually leads to the problem of misclassification. In FSOD, we notice the false positive (FP) of novel categories is prominent, in which the base categories are often recognized as novel ones. We propose a crop-paste augmentation pipeline that generates synthetic training samples by extracting high-quality instance crops from base classes and pasting them into diverse scenes to broaden the visual appearance of novel categories while preserving label integrity. A context-aware paste module enforces geometric and semantic plausibility, using scale- and location-aware pasting, a lightweight paste-discriminator, and stratified background sampling to maintain contextual realism. To curb misclassification, we integrate a decoupled detection head and a calibration objective that separates base and novel predictions and penalizes base objects being labeled as novel, complemented by adaptive inference thresholds. The pipeline can be appended to standard FSOD frameworks as a plug-in augmentation without re-training from scratch. Empirical results on PASCAL VOC and MS COCO across 1-, 3-, and 5-shot settings show consistent gains in novel-AP and a substantial reduction in false positives stemming from base-as-novel misclassifications, while preserving base performance. Ablation studies highlight the importance of paste scale, context fidelity, and negative mining, with the method yielding roughly 3–7 point gains in AP_novel and up to 15–20% reductions in FP base-as-novel. Moreover, the approach demonstrates robustness to shot setting and domain shifts, offering a simple, lightweight, and scalable solution for practitioners seeking reliable few-shot detectors.
prefix: Few-shot object detection (FSOD) aims to expand an object detector for novel categories given only a few instances for training. However, detecting novel categories with only a few samples usually leads to the problem of misclassification. In FSOD, we notice the false positive (FP) of novel categories is prominent, in which the base categories are often recognized as novel ones.

title: QCD against BlackHoles of Stellar Mass
text_ai: In course of the consolidation of nucleon (neutron) spacing inside a compact star, two key factors are expected to come into play side by side: the lack of self-stabilization against shutting into black hole (BH) and forthcoming phase transition - color deconfinement and QCD-vacuum reconstruction - within the nuclear matter the star is composed of. To this end we formulate a microphysical framework that couples a hadronic phase to a deconfined quark matter core, employing a two-phase construction with a Gibbs or Maxwell approach depending on surface tension, and incorporating color-superconducting gaps in the quark sector. The hadronic sector is based on a relativistic mean-field description with density-dependent couplings; the quark sector adopts a bag-model parameterization augmented by a CFL-like pairing gap and a running QCD vacuum energy term. We explore a range of transition densities and surface tensions to map the stability landscape of stellar configurations. Mass–radius relations are computed through Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff integration, and the onset of instability is assessed via radial oscillation analysis. The analysis reveals that a stiff deconfined phase with a sizable pairing gap can raise the maximum mass by a few tenths of a solar mass, thereby allowing compact stars to withstand beyond traditional hadronic limits, consistent with observations of high-mass neutron stars. Conversely, if the transition is delayed or the EoS softens at onset, rapid collapse to a black hole becomes favored, imprinting signatures in the gravitational-wave spectrum and potential electromagnetic transients. Our results indicate that QCD vacuum reconstruction within dense matter acts as a stabilizing agent against stellar-mass BH formation, with measurable consequences for the demographics of compact objects and for the interpretation of transient astrophysical events.

title: ImmuNeCS: Neural Committee Search by an Artificial Immune System
text_ai: Current Neural Architecture Search techniques can suffer from a few shortcomings, including high computational cost, excessive bias from the search space, conceptual complexity or uncertain empirical benefits over random search. ImmuNeCS introduces a population-based search that evolves a repertoire of architectural antibodies rather than a single winner. Each antibody encodes a modular neural cell-stack with a compact genotype enabling recombination of blocks, skip connections, and width configurations. An antigen, defined by the task distribution and a small validation budget, provides a fitness signal via a surrogate performance predictor trained across tasks. Affinity is updated as partial training performance on a budgeted proxy, and antibodies with higher affinity undergo clonal expansion and somatic hypermutation to explore neighboring configurations. Recombination fuses compatible modules from top performers, yielding novel architectures with preserved validity. To sustain diversity, ImmuNeCS imposes a diversity regularizer and maintains an archive of structurally distinct antibodies. The resulting neural committee is formed by selecting a diverse, high-affinity subset and aggregating their predictions via a learned gating network or averaging, calibrated on a held-out set. This committee perspective affords robust inference under distributional shift and hardware constraints, and reduces the risk tied to single-architecture bets. Efficiency is achieved via a one-shot supernet with weight-sharing, early stopping, and budget-aware progression. The search optimizes accuracy, latency, and parameter count, yielding Pareto-efficient ensembles. We evaluate ImmuNeCS on established NAS benchmarks (NAS-Bench-201, NAS-Bench-101) and DARTS-like spaces, showing competitive or superior accuracy at a fraction of the compute, with improved reliability across seeds. The immune-inspired dynamics provide a principled mechanism to escape local optima, sustain exploration, and reveal reusable architectural motifs captured by the committee.

title: TeraHertz Band Communication: An Old Problem Revisited and Research Directions for the Next Decade
text_ai: Terahertz (THz) band communications are envisioned as a key technology for 6G and Beyond. As a fundamental wireless infrastructure, THz communication can boost abundant promising applications. In 2014, our team published two comprehensive roadmaps for the development and progress of THz communication networks [1], [2], which helped the research community to start research on this subject afterwards. Since those roadmaps, progress has matured in channel measurement campaigns, device technologies, and system-level design, yet fundamental bottlenecks persist. This work surveys the state of the art, harmonizes modeling approaches, and delineates a coherent research agenda for the coming decade. We summarize advances in THz transceivers, frontend RFICs, and materials-driven packaging, including approaches for CMOS/III–V integration and photonics-enabled links. We analyze propagation characteristics—molecular absorption, rain attenuation, and phase stability under urban, indoor, and vehicular conditions—and discuss implications for beam management, scalable MIMO, and robust coding. We address network architectures from ultra-dense THz access to THz backhaul/fronthaul, cross-layer optimization, and learning-enabled control. Finally, we chart prioritized challenges and milestones to catalyze standardized regimes, coordinated measurement campaigns, and open testbeds that can accelerate experimentation and deployment. This integrative perspective highlights cross-disciplinary gaps and concrete milestones to align academia, industry, and standardization bodies.

title: Reverberation and photoionization estimates of the Broad Line Region Radius in Low-z Quasars
text_ai: Black Hole Mass (M_BH) estimation in quasars, especially at high redshift, involves use of single epoch spectra with s/n and resolution that permit accurate measurement of the width of a broad line assumed to be a reliable virial estimator. Coupled with an estimate of the radius of the broad line region this yields M_BH. Reverberation mapping provides the most direct probe of the BLR size by measuring the lag between continuum fluctuations and the line response, thereby calibrating the R_BLR–L relation independent of geometry. Here we report a joint analysis that exploits both reverberation and photoionization information to estimate R_BLR in low-z quasars. Our approach uses lag measurements when available and supplements them with photoionization-derived radii for objects lacking reverberation. The latter are constrained with density- and ionization-sensitive diagnostics in optical spectra, interpreted through photoionization grids to infer the ionization parameter U and hydrogen density n_H. The ionizing photon rate Q(H) is estimated from the reconstructed continuum, enabling R_BLR,PI = Q(H)/(4π c n_H U). We apply this framework primarily to the Hβ line, and to Mg II, to test consistency across lines. We compare R_BLR,RM and R_BLR,PI and examine their coherence as a function of luminosity, Eddington ratio, and continuum shape; we also assess the role of radiation pressure and BLR geometry in the virial factor f used for M_BH. The joint radii yield black hole masses with reduced systematic biases relative to single-epoch R–L calibrations, particularly at the low-z end where host contamination and line blending are challenging. These radii enable cross-calibration of line-based M_BH across surveys and redshifts, testing R_BLR universality in the local universe. Our results indicate a unified view in which reverberation and photoionization radii trace a common BLR structure, with implications for local black hole demographics.

title: Quantile LSTM: A Robust LSTM for Anomaly Detection In Time Series Data
text_ai: Anomalies refer to the departure of systems and devices from their normal behaviour in standard operating conditions. An anomaly in an industrial device can indicate an upcoming failure, often in the temporal direction. In this paper, we make two contributions: 1) we estimate conditional quantiles and consider three different ways to define anomalies based on the estimated quantiles. To address this, we propose Quantile LSTM, a robust recurrent architecture that learns a family of conditional quantiles qα(y_t | x_t) for future observations by adding multiple quantile heads to an LSTM and training with the pinball loss. A monotonicity regularizer enforces non-crossing, producing coherent predictive intervals. For anomaly detection, we define three complementary criteria based on the estimated quantiles: (i) absolute-exceedance, flagging events when y_t falls outside the central interval defined by the α- and (1−α)-quantiles; (ii) quantile-residual exceedance, where the residual relative to the interval exceeds a data-driven threshold; (iii) temporal-interval breach, detecting sustained deviations via consecutive quantile violations. We validate on three real industrial datasets with varying noise and nonstationarity, comparing against strong LSTM, ARIMA, and kernel-based baselines. The results show improved precision-recall, fewer false alarms, and earlier warnings, with robustness to outliers and non-Gaussian noise.

title: Visibility of current and shot noise in electrical Mach-Zehnder and Hanbury Brown Twiss interferometers
text_ai: We investigate the visibility of the current and shot-noise correlations of electrical analogs of the optical Mach-Zehnder interferometer and the Hanbury Brown Twiss interferometer. The electrical analogs are discussed in conductors subject to high magnetic fields where electron motion is along edge states. The transport quantities are modulated with the help of an Aharonov-Bohm flux. We formulate the circuits within the Landauer-Büttiker framework for chiral quantum Hall edge channels and derive expressions for the flux-dependent current and zero-frequency cross-correlations. In the Mach-Zehnder setup, the current at the drains shows AB oscillations whose visibility is governed by the beam-splitter transparencies and by dephasing mechanisms. We treat dephasing either through a phenomenological phase-averaging over a distribution of Aharonov-Bohm phases or via fictitious probes, recovering a monotonic suppression of visibility with temperature or voltage. In the Hanbury Brown–Twiss geometry, the cross-correlations reveal two-particle interference: AB-modulated shot noise with a visibility that reflects fermionic antibunching and the partitioning of edge channels. We contrast current and noise visibilities, identifying parameter regimes where shot-noise visibility can exceed current-visibility and where phase averaging dominates. The results supply experimental benchmarks for visibility control in electrical interferometers based on quantum Hall edge states.

title: Depinning and flow of a vortex line in an uniaxial random medium
text_ai: We study numerically and analytically the dynamics of a single directed elastic string driven through a 3-dimensional disordered medium. In the quasistatic limit the string is super-rough in the driving direction, with roughness exponent $\zeta_{\parallel} = 1.25\pm 0.01$, dynamic exponent $z_{\parallel}= 1.43 \pm 0.01$, correlation-length exponent $\nu= 1.33 \pm 0.02$, depinning exponent $\beta = 0.24\pm 0.01$, and avalanche-size exponent $\tau_{\parallel} = 1.09 \pm 0.03$. Beyond the quasistatic regime the line exhibits a finite depinning threshold F_c and a continuous transition to a flowing state. Near F_c the correlation length diverges as ξ ∼ |F − F_c|^{−ν} with ν = 1.33 ± 0.02, while times scale as t ∼ ξ^{z_parallel} with z_parallel = 1.43 ± 0.01. The driving-direction roughness remains super-rough, ζ_parallel ≈ 1.25 ± 0.01; transverse fluctuations are weaker, ζ_perp = 0.60 ± 0.04, yielding an anisotropy χ ≈ 2.1. The structure factor separates into S(k_parallel) ∼ k_parallel^{−(1+2ζ_parallel)} and S(k_perp) ∼ k_perp^{−(1+2ζ_perp)} with data collapse confirming universal anisotropic scaling. Avalanche statistics give P(S) ∼ S^{−τ_parallel} with τ_parallel = 1.09 ± 0.03 and a size cutoff S_c ∼ L^{D} with D ≈ 1.75, consistent with fractal avalanches. Overall, the results agree with a one-loop FRG description for a 1D elastic line in uniaxially disordered 3D media, defining a distinct universality class from isotropic disorder. These findings provide a benchmark for experiments on layered superconductors. Future work will explore finite-temperature rounding and crossovers to creep in weak-drive regimes. These results invite experimental tests.

title: Do people's user types change over time? An exploratory study
text_ai: In recent years, different studies have proposed and validated user models (e.g., Bartle, BrainHex, and Hexad) to represent the different user profiles in games and gamified settings. However, the results of applying these user models in practice (e.g., to personalize gamified systems) are still contradictory. To investigate temporal stability, we conducted a longitudinal deployment in a gamified learning environment with 128 participants across eight weeks, administering the Hexad, BrainHex, and Bartle inventories at four evenly spaced points. We supplemented quantitative measures with qualitative prompts about perceived changes in motivation and behavior. Stability was assessed via test-retest reliability (ICC) and transitions between adjacent types. Findings reveal partial but heterogeneous temporal stability across models. In Hexad, Achievers and Philanthropists showed moderate stability (ICC around 0.6–0.7), whereas Free Spirits and Socializers exhibited greater fluctuation aligned with exposure to social mechanics. BrainHex and Bartle produced broadly similar patterns, with Explorer-dominated profiles most stable; Daredevil-leaning profiles were more prone to drift. Contextual factors—especially feature exposure, task fit, and prior experience—significantly moderated drift. The results challenge the assumption of fixed user types and underscore the value of adaptive, decay-aware profiling in personalization pipelines. Limitations include single-domain sampling; generalizability and causal mechanisms warrant further study.

title: Non-union of the ulnar styloid process in children is common but long-term morbidity is rare: a population-based study with mean 11 years (9-15) follow-up.
text_ai: Background and purpose - Fracture of the ulnar styloid process (USP) is common in children in connection with distal radius fracture. The long-term morbidity of USP non-union following a childhood distal radius fracture is unclear. We evaluated long-term clinical and radiographic findings of USP non-union. Materials and methods - We conducted a population-based cohort study using regional radiographic archives to identify children (aged 5–15 years at injury) with distal radius fracture accompanied by USP non-union. Inclusion required radiographic evidence of USP discontinuity persisting beyond 6 months. Medical records were reviewed, and survivors were invited for long-term clinical and radiographic reevaluation. Clinical assessment encompassed pain on palpation and activity, wrist range of motion (flexion–extension, pronation–supination), grip strength (dynamometer), and standardized patient-reported outcomes (PODCI). Radiographic evaluation focused on USP status, radiocarpal alignment, secondary signs of instability, and degenerative changes. Follow-up was mean 11 years (range 9–15). Descriptive statistics described cohort characteristics. Comparative analyses used paired or independent t tests for continuous outcomes and chi-square tests for categorical outcomes, with linear mixed models to adjust for age and sex where appropriate. Significance was set at P < 0.05. Results - Radiographic USP non-union persisted in the majority of cases at long-term follow-up, yet clinically significant symptoms were uncommon. Pain during daily activities or at rest was reported by only a minority, and no persistent pain or nocturnal symptoms were observed. Range of motion and grip strength of the injured wrist were comparable to the contralateral side and to normative pediatric data. PODCI scores indicated preserved function and activity participation in most patients. No consistent predictors of morbidity emerged from fracture characteristics, treatment modality, or initial displacement. Conclusion - In this population, USP non-union after pediatric distal radius fracture is radiographically frequent but clinically inconsequential in the long term, supporting conservative management in asymptomatic individuals.

The long-term morbidity of USP non-union following a childhood distal radius fracture is unclear. We evaluated long-term clinical and radiographic findings of USP non-union.

title: Does the Presence of Risk Factors for Fetal Growth Restriction Increase the Probability of Antenatal Detection? A French National Study.
text_ai: Screening for fetal growth restriction (FGR) is a major component of prenatal care. We investigated whether the presence of maternal and pregnancy risk factors for FGR improves the antenatal suspicion of FGR for infants born small-for-gestational age (SGA) as well as their impact on screening specificity. Methods: We conducted a nationwide cohort analysis using linked national perinatal data from singleton pregnancies delivering between 2010 and 2018. FGR was defined as birthweight <10th percentile for gestational age; antenatal detection was captured when antenatal records documented suspected FGR or when ultrasound-estimated fetal weight fell below the corresponding threshold. Maternal and pregnancy risk factors for FGR included smoking during pregnancy, advanced maternal age, pregestational diabetes, chronic hypertension or preeclampsia, nulliparity, and a history of prior FGR. Sensitivity of antenatal suspicion for FGR was calculated among infants born SGA, stratified by the presence of risk factors, while specificity was estimated among infants not born SGA. Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for gestational age at delivery, fetal sex, parity, maternal body mass index, and center clustering. 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported for all estimates. Results: Of approximately 1.5 million singleton births, 135 000 (9%) were SGA. Antenatal suspicion of FGR was recorded in about 41% of SGA infants. In pregnancies with at least one FGR risk factor (n ≈ 70 000), antenatal suspicion occurred in ~40% (≈28 000), whereas among those without risk factors (n ≈ 65 000) it occurred in ~20% (≈13 000). The adjusted odds ratio for antenatal suspicion in SGA births with risk factors versus without was 2.5 (95% CI 2.3–2.7). Among non-SGA infants (n ≈ 1 365 000), antenatal suspicion was more frequent in pregnancies with risk factors (≈2.5%) than in those without (≈0.9%), translating into a decrease in screening specificity from 98.7% to 96.9% (p<0.001). Conclusions: The presence of FGR risk factors strengthens antenatal detection in infants who are ultimately born SGA but modestly reduces screening specificity due to increased suspicion in non-SGA pregnancies. These findings support risk-stratified screening approaches that integrate targeted ultrasound assessment and Doppler evaluation to optimize detection of FGR while limiting excess false positives in low-risk pregnancies.

title: A Reinforcement Learning Approach to Parameter Selection for Distributed Optimal Power Flow
text_ai: With the increasing penetration of distributed energy resources, distributed optimization algorithms have attracted significant attention for power systems applications due to their potential for superior scalability, privacy, and robustness to a single point-of-failure. The Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) is a popular distributed optimization algorithm; however, its convergence performance is highly dependent on the selection of penalty parameters, which are usually chosen heuristically. We formulate the penalty selection as a learning control problem and introduce a reinforcement learning policy that prescribes per-iteration ADMM penalty updates for distributed AC-OPF. The state includes current primal and dual residuals, objective gap, constraint violations, and lightweight local observables such as line flows and generator setpoints; actions adjust penalty values, with per-zone adaptations and temporal smoothing. A graph neural network policy exploits network topology to generalize across sizes and topologies, trained offline on a curated ensemble of networks and operating points. Compared with fixed penalties and heuristic adaptive schemes, RL-tuned ADMM achieves faster convergence and more reliable feasibility, reducing iteration counts and time while preserving quality objectives. The approach preserves privacy, scales with system size, and remains robust to moderate modeling error and measurement noise.

title: Reproductive Coercion Among African American Female Adolescents: Associations with Contraception and Sexually Transmitted Diseases.
text_ai: Background: Among adolescents, racial disparities in reproductive health outcomes persist. The question of whether reproductive coercion (RC) influences these outcomes has received increased attention. Little is known about whether RC is independently associated with contraceptive use and having a sexually transmitted disease (STD) among African American female adolescents. Objectives: To examine whether RC is independently associated with contraception use and with self-reported history of an STD among African American female adolescents. Methods: Cross-sectional baseline data were analyzed from 412 African American female adolescents aged 14–19 recruited from urban clinics and community settings. RC was measured with a validated scale capturing birth-control sabotage and coercive pregnancy pressure. Contraception use at last sex was categorized as any method, dual-method use, or no method. An STD in the past year was self-reported clinical diagnosis. Covariates included age, education, insurance status, relationship type, dating violence, and gynecologic history. Multivariable logistic regression estimated associations of RC (high vs low/none) with contraception non-use and STD history, adjusting for covariates. Results: High RC was endorsed by 24% of participants. After adjustment, RC was independently associated with lower odds of any contraception use (AOR 0.60, 95% CI 0.44–0.82) and higher odds of a past-year STD (AOR 2.05, 95% CI 1.28–3.28). RC also predicted inconsistent condom use (AOR 1.78, 95% CI 1.15–2.75). The RC–STD association persisted after accounting for contraception use (AOR 1.72, 95% CI 1.05–2.84). Conclusions: RC is an independent risk factor for contraception non-use and STD history among African American female adolescents. RC screening and counseling in clinical and community settings, with strategies to support autonomous contraception and confidential access, may help reduce disparities. Future work should evaluate intervention models that integrate RC assessment into teen-friendly reproductive health services.

title: Distributed generalized Nash equilibria computation of monotone games via a preconditioned proximal point algorithm
text_ai: In this paper, we investigate distributed generalized Nash equilibrium (GNE) computation of monotone games with affine coupling constraints. Each player can only utilize its local objective function, local feasible set and a local block of the coupling constraint, and can only communicate with its neighbours. Building on the monotone game formulation, we derive a distributed preconditioned proximal point algorithm (D-PPPA) that uses only local data and neighbour communication. Each agent performs a proximal substep that incorporates its local objective, a local projection onto its feasible set, and a consensus term for the affine coupling, followed by an update of the dual multipliers associated with the coupling constraints. The method employs a network-aware preconditioner encoding the incidence structure and connectivity, enabling blockwise updates that can be executed in parallel. We prove that, under standard convexity and monotonicity assumptions and with an appropriate choice of step-sizes, the induced operator is averaged, ensuring convergence to a variational GNE. We obtain a sublinear O(1/k) convergence rate in the ergodic sense, and linear convergence under strong monotonicity or strong convexity of the local objectives. Numerical experiments on distributed resource allocation and network games illustrate scalability, low per-iteration communication, and robustness to moderate asynchrony and time-varying graphs.

title: Status of the Medium-Sized Telescopes for the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory
text_ai: The Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory (CTAO) is a next-generation ground-based gamma-ray observatory that will study the universe at very high energy using atmospheric Cherenkov light. CTAO will comprise over 67 telescopes of three different sizes, located in the northern and southern hemispheres. This paper reviews the status of the Medium-Sized Telescopes (MSTs) that comprise the heart of the CTAO's sensitivity in the 100 GeV–10 TeV regime. After an extensive technical design review, the MST baseline of 12 m Davies-Cotton optics has progressed through the production and qualification of mirror facets, structure, drive systems, and calibration hardware, with several pre-production units undergoing integrated tests at national test facilities and on-sky demonstrations. The dual-path development includes continuation of the DC-MST program and parallel evaluation of alternative designs (e.g., dual-mirror, compact SC-based concepts) to optimize electronic and optical packaging, field-of-view, and cost-per-channel. The camera chain has achieved milestones in sensor technology, front-end electronics, real-time triggering, and data acquisition, with validation against end-to-end simulations and CTA data models. An emphasis on reliability under harsh environmental conditions has driven improvements in mirror coating longevity, protective enclosures, and remote diagnostics. On-site deployment in both hemispheres remains on track, with site-specific integration campaigns coordinated across international consortia, town planning, and safety reviews. Early commissioning activities have demonstrated stable pointing, accurate optical alignment, and robust data transfer, while calibration pipelines and instrument-response functions are being refined against a growing data set of standard candles and Monte Carlo benchmarks. The status reported here indicates that MSTs are meeting performance goals, with projected readiness for full array integration aligned to the CTAO construction and science program.

title: Illustrating the Applicability of IRT to Implementation Science: Examining an Instrument of Therapist Attitudes.
text_ai: Pragmatic instruments with psychometric support are important to advance dissemination and implementation (D&I) research, but few well-researched D&I instruments exist. Item response theory (IRT), an approach that is underutilized in D&I, can help with the development of actionable and brief instruments. In this study, we illustrate the application of IRT to an instrument assessing therapist attitudes toward implementing evidence-based practices. We collected data from therapists employed in community-based settings across contexts. We fit both unidimensional and multidimensional IRT models to item responses, evaluated item fit, and examined item information across the latent attitude continuum. Results showed that several items functioned with high discrimination and substantial information in the moderate-to-strongly favorable attitude range, while others contributed little information and displayed ceiling effects. We generated a shortened scale by selecting high-information items, preserving domains, and verified measurement invariance across clinician discipline, years of experience, and site. The resulting instrument demonstrated improved precision at decision points for uptake of new practices and provided a reliable brief form for screening in D&I studies. We discuss implications for instrument development, practical deployment, and future use of IRT to refine pragmatic measures in implementation science.

title: Artificial intelligence in government: Concepts, standards, and a unified framework
text_ai: Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), especially in generative language modelling, hold the promise of transforming government. Given the advanced capabilities of new AI systems, it is critical that these are embedded using standard operational procedures, clear epistemic criteria, and behave in alignment with the normative expectations of society. To this end, we develop a unified framework that integrates governance principles, technical standards, and evaluation practices across public contexts. The framework rests on three layers: normative alignment (ethical, legal, human-rights), technical integrity (robustness, security, transparency), and procedural accountability (auditing, oversight, public engagement). We map decision rights and accountability lines to institutional roles, prescribing model lifecycle processes from problem articulation and data stewardship to deployment, monitoring, and retirement. Standardized artefacts—risk registers, data dictionaries, model cards, and impact assessments—are embedded to enable reproducibility and cross-agency interoperability. Drawing on existing international norms (ISO/IEC AI standards, NIST AI RMF, OECD principles, and EU regulatory proposals), the framework extends them with a taxonomy that supports risk-informed procurement, governance-by-design, and continuous assurance. It also articulates a test-bench methodology for evaluating capability, fairness, explainability, and resilience under adversarial conditions, coupled with human-in-the-loop controls. Data governance is anchored in provenance, quality, consent, and reuse constraints, with mechanisms for redress and red-teaming. The contribution offers a practical blueprint for policymakers, agencies, and contractors to align AI-enabled services with public-interest objectives while maintaining interoperability and auditability. It supports scenario-based governance, structured risk articulation, and scalable certification pathways, thereby bridging research, standards development, and administrative practice toward trustworthy government AI, guiding implementation, oversight, and ongoing public deliberation.

Given the advanced capabilities of new AI systems, it is critical that these are embedded using standard operational procedures, clear epistemic criteria, and behave in alignment with the normative expectations of society.

title: Palette-colouring: a belief-propagation approach
text_ai: We consider a variation of the prototype combinatorial-optimisation problem known as graph-colouring. Our optimisation goal is to colour the vertices of a graph with a fixed number of colours, in a way to maximise the number of different colours present in the set of nearest neighbours of each given vertex. We formulate the optimization on factor graphs and derive Belief-Propagation (BP) equations for the marginal probabilities of vertex-colour assignments. The objective is encoded by a local-pairwise potential that rewards diversity in colours occupying a vertex’s neighbourhood; yielding a replica-symmetric fixed point. We then employ a BP-guided decimation (BP-Dec) scheme: at each step, the most biased vertex is fixed to its highest-probability colour and BP is restarted on reduced instance. To improve robustness, damping and random restarts are used, yielding a heuristic with polynomial-time complexity. We benchmark on ensembles of random graphs varying average degree and palette size, comparing with standard palette heuristics. The results reveal a phase-like behaviour: in sparse regimes, several fixed points coexist and convergence slows; in denser regimes, a fixed point emerges, delivering substantial palette diversity. The approach scales to graphs of size and provides a solver for palette-colouring.
prefix: We consider a variation of the prototype combinatorial-optimisation problem known as graph-colouring. Our optimisation goal is to colour the vertices of a graph with a fixed number of colours, in a way to maximise the number of different colours present in the set of nearest neighbours of each given vertex.

title: Articulatory Representation Learning Via Joint Factor Analysis and Neural Matrix Factorization
text_ai: Articulatory representation learning is the fundamental research in modeling neural speech production system. Our previous work has established a deep paradigm to decompose the articulatory kinematics data into gestures, which explicitly model the phonological and linguistic structure encoded with human speech production mechanism, and corresponding gestural scores. Building on this foundation, we introduce a joint factor analysis and neural matrix factorization (JFA-NMF) framework that simultaneously learns an interpretable gesture basis and a latent matrix factorization of articulatory trajectories across speakers and contexts. By factorizing the observed kinematics into a low-dimensional gesture latent and a flexible multiplicative speaker–context component, the model captures coarticulatory dynamics while preserving phonological structure. The joint objective combines a probabilistic factor-analysis term with a neural matrix factorization reconstruction term, augmented by sparsity and temporal regularizers. A shared gesture dictionary encodes canonical articulatory gestures, while neural factors adapt to speaker identity and speaking rate, enabling zero-shot generalization to unseen speakers and phoneme sequences. We evaluate on multi-speaker EMA datasets and synthetic controls, showing superior reconstruction fidelity, improved gesture interpretability, and enhanced downstream task performance in articulatory-to-acoustic synthesis and recognition. The approach yields compact, disentangled representations that illuminate the organization of speech production.
prefix: Articulatory representation learning is the fundamental research in modeling neural speech production system. Our previous work has established a deep paradigm to decompose the articulatory kinematics data into gestures, which explicitly model the phonological and linguistic structure encoded with human speech production mechanism, and corresponding gestural scores.

title: Prevalence of mecA on oral mucosa in patients undergoing hematopoietic stem cell transplantation
text_ai: Objectives: Severe oral mucositis occurring after hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HCT) is associated with a risk of systemic infection related to bacteremia. We reported antibiotic-resistant bacteria detected on the oral mucosa frequently during the period of HCT and indicated an association between oral mucositis and antibiotic-resistant bacterial infection (2011 MASCC/ISOO Annual Meeting). Methods: In a prospective cohort of adults undergoing HSCT at [institution], oral mucosa swabs were collected at three time points: baseline (pre-conditioning), onset of mucositis (WHO grade >1), and neutrophil recovery. mecA was detected by real-time PCR targeting the mecA gene and by culture for confirmation; species were identified by MALDI-TOF. A positive mecA result was defined as detection in any oral mucosal sample. Clinical data included conditioning regimen, antibiotic exposure during admission, mucositis grading, duration of neutropenia, and incidence of bacteremia with mecA-positive organisms. Analyses included prevalence estimation, logistic regression for risk factors of mecA carriage, and Fisher’s exact tests for associations with mucositis severity. Results: Among 120 enrolled patients, mecA was detected in the oral mucosa of 32 (27%) at least once. Detection frequency increased during grade 3–4 mucositis (42%) compared with grade 0–2 (18%), P=0.006. Independent risk factors for mecA carriage were recent broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure (OR 3.2, 95% CI 1.5–6.7) and prolonged neutropenia (>10 days) (OR 2.1, 95% CI 1.0–4.6). Coagulase-negative staphylococci accounted for 68% of mecA-positive isolates. Bacteremia due to mecA-positive organisms occurred in 3 patients, all with prior oral mecA detection (P=0.04). Rates of bacteremia due to mecA-negative organisms did not differ by colonization status. Conclusions: mecA carriage on oral mucosa is common in HSCT, particularly during severe mucositis and after antibiotic exposure, and may precede bloodstream infection by mecA-positive pathogens. Oral mecA surveillance could inform stewardship and mucositis management in HCT recipients.

We reported antibiotic-resistant bacteria detected on the oral mucosa frequently during the period of HCT and indicated an association between oral mucositis and antibiotic-resistant bacterial infection (2011 MASCC/ISOO Annual Meeting).

title: Proportional Dynamics in Linear Fisher Markets with Auto-bidding: Convergence, Incentives and Fairness
text_ai: Proportional dynamics, originated from peer-to-peer file sharing systems, models a decentralized price-learning process in Fisher markets. Previously, items in the dynamics operate independently of one another, and each is assumed to belong to a different seller. Extending the framework to general Fisher markets with a seller owning several items, we study a continuous-time proportional price-update rule combined with automatic demand responses (auto-bidding) of buyers who maximize linear utilities under budgets. Each item’s price evolves according to its own excess demand, while buyers reallocate spending automatically to bundles as prices change. We prove convergence to the Fisher market equilibrium under linear utilities from any positive initial prices and endowments; the convergence is exponential under gross-substitute. We further characterize the incentives induced by auto-bidding. In particular, unilateral misreporting of item ownership or price can only degrade a seller’s payoff at equilibrium; we derive bounds on potential gains from manipulation and identify regimes where truthful reporting forms a Nash equilibrium. Regarding fairness, limit allocation is envy-free among buyers and satisfies proportional fairness, coinciding with the competitive equilibrium allocation and attaining Pareto efficiency. Numerical experiments illustrate rapid convergence and robustness to budget heterogeneity, with fairness preserved.

title: Short-ranged interaction effects on $Z_2$ topological phase transitions: The perturbative mean-field method
text_ai: Time-reversal symmetric topological insulator is a novel state of matter that a bulk-insulating state carries dissipationless spin transport along the surfaces, embedded by the $Z_2$ topological invariant. In the noninteracting limit, this exotic state has been intensively studied and explored with realistic systems, such as HgTe/(Hg,Cd)Te quantum wells. Here we implement the perturbative mean-field (PMF) scheme to treat short-range interactions within a lattice realization of a Z2 topological insulator. We consider the Bernevig–Hughes–Zhang (BHZ) model on a two-dimensional lattice augmented by on-site Hubbard U and a nearest-neighbor density-density repulsion V, both chosen to preserve time-reversal symmetry and charge conservation. Expanding the interaction in a controlled perturbative series in U/t and V/t and projecting onto the low-energy subspace yields an effective single-particle Hamiltonian H_eff(k) in which the mass term and the spin–orbit–coupled hoppings acquire self-consistent, interaction-dependent renormalizations. The PMF equations are solved self-consistently for uniform order parameters, and the Z2 topological invariant is tracked via the Fu–Kane parity criterion at time-reversal invariant momenta, complemented by edge-state spectra to confirm bulk–boundary correspondence. At weak coupling, we find a monotonic shift of the phase boundary: increasing U (and V) renormalizes M and can drive the system across the topological transition when the bulk gap closes at Gamma, X, or M points. In most parameter regimes, short-range repulsion reduces the extent of the TI phase, consistent with a tendency toward localization; however, for carefully tuned ratios of hopping and interaction, an interaction-assisted transition can occur, producing a reentrant behavior of the Z2 index. The results remain qualitatively robust against moderate variations in lattice details, suggesting that PMF captures essential physics of interaction-modulated Z2 transitions in realistic materials and designer platforms, including quantum-well arrays and cold-atom simulators where interaction scales are tunable.

title: $R^2$-Mesh: Reinforcement Learning Powered Mesh Reconstruction via Geometry and Appearance Refinement
text_ai: Mesh reconstruction based on Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) is popular in a variety of applications such as computer graphics, virtual reality, and medical imaging due to its efficiency in handling complex geometric structures and facilitating real-time rendering. However, existing works often fail to capture fine geometric details accurately and struggle with optimizing rendering quality. To address these limitations, we propose R^2-Mesh, a reinforcement-learning powered framework that jointly optimizes geometry and appearance under a NeRF-informed objective. We formulate mesh refinement as a Markov decision process in which an agent acts on a multi-resolution mesh, executing actions such as vertex perturbations, edge flips, face splits/merges, and attribute edits (color, reflectance). A geometry refinement module nudges vertex positions toward high-frequency geometric cues inferred from the neural radiance field, while an appearance refinement module learns per-face neural textures and BRDF parameters to suppress shading artifacts. The rendering loss couples photometric reconstruction with silhouette, normal, and edge-consistency terms, augmented by a regularization that favors smoothness and simplicity. Training alternates between differentiable rendering-based supervision and reinforcement-learning updates with a curriculum from coarse to fine meshes. Experiments on synthetic and real-scenes show superior geometry fidelity and appearance realism, with improved generalization and efficiency.

title: Continual Evolution in Nonreciprocal Ecological Models
text_ai: Feedbacks between evolution and ecology are ubiquitous, with ecological interactions determining which mutants are successful, and these mutants in turn modifying community structure. We study the evolutionary dynamics of several ecological models with overlapping niches, including consumer resource and Lotka-Volterra models. Across two canonical classes—consumer-resource models with overlapping resource spectra and Lotka-Volterra systems with asymmetrical interactions—we show that nonreciprocal feedbacks generically prevent convergence to a fixed ecological–genetic state. In the consumer-resource setting, invasion fitness depends on the current resource abundances, which are themselves sculpted by resident traits; this feedback creates a moving target that sustains directional selection and continual trait displacement. In nonreciprocal Lotka-Volterra models, antisymmetric components of the interaction matrix remove the gradient structure that would otherwise stabilize equilibria, yielding limit cycles, quasi-periodic motion, or chaotic itineraries in trait space. We identify a minimal set of quantitative conditions under which perpetual evolution arises: nonzero nonreciprocal couplings together with ecological recovery times that are finite but not vanishingly rapid relative to mutation timescales. When reciprocity is restored, or when mutation input is vanishingly small, the coevolutionary dynamics collapse to equilibria or to degenerate neutral drift. We complement analytic results with extensive simulations across dimensionalities and mutation regimes, showing robust Red Queen-like dynamics over broad parameter ranges. Spectral decomposition of the ecological Jacobian and perturbation theory provide tractable criteria predicting transitions between stationary, cyclic, and chaotic regimes, aligning with mean-field approximations. Our findings suggest continual evolution is a generic consequence of nonreciprocal ecological architecture and offers a unified explanation for persistent change observed in diverse communities. This motivates empirical tests of perpetual change.

We study the evolutionary dynamics of several ecological models with overlapping niches, including consumer resource and Lotka-Volterra models.

title: SL-YOLO: A Stronger and Lighter Drone Target Detection Model
text_ai: Detecting small objects in complex scenes, such as those captured by drones, is a daunting challenge due to the difficulty in capturing the complex features of small targets. While the YOLO family has achieved great success in large target detection, its performance is less than satisfactory when faced with small targets. SL-YOLO introduces a compact yet robust architecture tailored for UAV imagery with small targets. Its backbone preserves high-resolution features via a streamlined stage design and cross-stage connections. A Spatially Guided Feature Pyramid (SGFP) fuses multi-scale features via depthwise separable operations, preserving sharp spatial cues for tiny targets. The detection head uses an anchor-free, center-ness–aware regression with a light context module to suppress distractions. To enhance robustness, a lightweight attention block emphasizes object-centric regions without incurring heavy costs. Training leverages targeted augmentations (scale jitter, blur, photometric variation) and knowledge distillation from a larger teacher to transfer discriminative small-object cues. On VisDrone and UAVDT benchmarks, SL-YOLO delivers superior small-object AP while reducing parameters and FLOPs relative to strong baselines, and sustains near real-time inference on edge devices. These gains enable reliable deployment in surveillance, search-and-rescue, and environmental monitoring scenarios where real-time, accurate small-object detection is critical. The approach maintains compatibility with existing YOLO pipelines without sacrificing accuracy.

title: Computational insights and the observation of SiC nanograin assembly: towards 2D silicon carbide
text_ai: While an increasing number of two-dimensional (2D) materials, including graphene and silicene, have already been realized, others have only been predicted. An interesting example is the two-dimensional form of silicon carbide (2D-SiC). Here, we present an observation of atomically thin and hexagonally bonded nanosized grains of SiC assembling temporarily in graphene oxide pores during an atomic resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy experiment. To rationalize the observation, we combine in situ imaging with first-principles and kinetic modeling to identify nucleation and growth pathways under electron irradiation. Density functional theory calculations show that a Si–C honeycomb lattice (2D-SiC) can be stabilized at undercoordinated pore rims, with alternating Si and C terminations favored at oxide edges. Edge-passivation by O-containing groups reduces reconstruction energy and fosters hexagonal connectivity. Reactive molecular dynamics and metadynamics reveal rapid diffusion of Si and C species along graphene oxide pores and capture of clusters, consistent with the assemblies observed. A growth mechanism is proposed, wherein Si–C unit insertion at the rim leads to hexagonal grains that dissolve when beam-induced defect creation outpaces attachment. These insights point to beam-assisted routes for controlled 2D-SiC formation and integration in van der Waals heterostructures.

title: Paxos Made EPR: Decidable Reasoning about Distributed Protocols
text_ai: Distributed protocols such as Paxos play an important role in many computer systems. Therefore, a bug in a distributed protocol may have tremendous effects. Accordingly, a lot of effort has been invested in verifying such protocols. However, checking invariants of such protocols is undecidable and hard in practice, as it requires reasoning about an unbounded number of nodes and messages. In this work, we introduce Paxos Made EPR (PMEPR), a decidable, parameterized verification framework for Paxos-like protocols. We encode each role (proposer, acceptor, learner) with a compact collection of state predicates, and model unbounded participation by a finite domain of agents and a fixed set of message types. By restricting to a function-free, finite-signature representation, the encoding falls into the effectively propositional fragment EPR. Invariants are expressed as universally quantified Horn clauses over agent sorts; channels and histories are represented by a small number of relations with locality constraints that preserve a finite ground structure. We establish that a safety invariant holds for all sizes if the negation of the invariant yields an unsatisfiable EPR problem, enabling automatic verification with standard EPR decision procedures. When a counterexample is produced, a counterexample-guided refinement loop adds inductive strengthenings, preserving decidability while increasing expressiveness. We instantiate PMEPR on several Paxos variants, verifying Agreement for arbitrary numbers of participants and under practical optimizations such as Multi-Paxos and reconfiguration. We implemented a tool chain that translates high-level Paxos specifications into EPR and automates verification using existing decidability engines; experiments demonstrate scalable parameterized verification for nontrivial configurations and provide a practical pathway to formal safety proofs for distributed protocols.

title: Multi-Tracer Correlated Stacking: A Novel Way to Discover Anisotropy in nano-Hz Stochastic Gravitational Wave Background
text_ai: The isotropic stochastic gravitational wave background (SGWB) generated by a population of supermassive black hole binaries (SMBHBs) provides a unique window into their cosmic evolution. In addition to the isotropic power spectrum, the anisotropic component of the signal carries additional information about the supermassive black holes (SMBHs) and host galaxy connection. By combining the angular information encoded in multiple tracers—galaxy density fields, AGN catalogs, and star-forming galaxy maps—the MTCS estimator coherently stacks the directional signatures imprinted by SMBHBs onto the nano-Hz GW background. We construct angular templates from each catalog, including selection functions and sky masks, and form a joint multi-tracer likelihood for the anisotropic coefficients a_{lm}. The correlated stacking integrates timing residuals across the pulsar array not only by their angular separation but also by their expected correlation with each tracer, thereby reducing cosmic variance and mitigating tracer-specific systematics. We validate the framework with simulations of PTA data, including a populated SMBHB sky map generating a realistic anisotropic SGWB, pulsar timing noise, red noise, and a stochastic isotropic component. The estimator successfully recovers input a_{lm} up to l≈2–3 with uncertainties dominated by pulsar count and tracer density, and yields order-unity improvements in detection significance for moderate anisotropy levels compared to single-tracer analyses. We demonstrate that the multi-tracer approach breaks degeneracies between the isotropic amplitude and anisotropic coefficients and enables joint inference of SMBHB merger rates, mass function, and the SMBH–host connection. Our results indicate that ongoing IPTA data releases and upcoming SKA-era PTA observations will be capable of detecting and characterizing nano-Hz anisotropy with this method, unlocking astrophysical information on galaxy evolution and SMBH assembly.

In addition to the isotropic power spectrum, the anisotropic component of the signal carries additional information about the supermassive black holes (SMBHs) and host galaxy connection.

title: Cycle-SUM: Cycle-consistent Adversarial LSTM Networks for Unsupervised Video Summarization
text_ai: In this paper, we present a novel unsupervised video summarization model that requires no manual annotation. The proposed model termed Cycle-SUM adopts a new cycle-consistent adversarial LSTM architecture that can effectively maximize the information preserving and compactness of the summary video. It consists of a frame selector and a cycle-consistent learning based evaluator. Both components are trained jointly in an end-to-end unsupervised objective. The frame selector uses an LSTM-based policy to assign saliency scores and produce a compact sequence that preserves events of interest. The cycle-consistent evaluator comprises a forward reconstructor that reconstructs the original video from the selected frames and a backward reconstructor that recovers the selection from the reconstruction. A cycle-consistency loss enforces bidirectional reconstruction, while an adversarial discriminator promotes realism and temporal coherence. Additional penalties promote sparsity of selections and minimize redundancy. Empirical results on SumMe and TVSum show that Cycle-SUM surpasses strong unsupervised baselines, with robust performance across varied lengths. Beyond quantitative gains, the framework yields diverse summaries that cover salient events with minimal redundancy across varied video genres. We publish the code and provide a detailed ablation analysis to illustrate the contribution of each component.

The proposed model termed Cycle-SUM adopts a new cycle-consistent adversarial LSTM architecture that can effectively maximize the information preserving and compactness of the summary video. It consists of a frame selector and a cycle-consistent learning based evaluator.

title: Broad-band spectral study of LMXB black hole candidate 4U 1957+11 with NuSTAR
text_ai: We present here the results of broadband spectral analysis of low-mass X-ray binary and a black hole candidate 4U 1957+11. The source was observed nine times with the Nuclear Spectroscopic Telescope Array (NuSTAR) between 2018 September and 2019 November. During these observations, the spectral state of 4U 1957+11 evolved marginally. We fitted the 3–79 keV spectra with a diskbb plus a thermally Comptonized tail (nthcomp), allowing for relativistic blurring when required, and fixed Galactic absorption (tbabs). Across epochs, the spectra remained soft, with the disk contributing the majority of the 0.5–10 keV flux and the Comptonized tail accounting for the remainder up to the NuSTAR band. The disk temperature varied around 0.6–0.9 keV, the coronal photon index near 2.3–2.6, and the electron temperature was weakly constrained, with lower limits of tens of keV and cutoffs around 50–100 keV. Reflection signatures were marginal or absent, and the Fe K region showed no compelling features. The inferred inner disk radius remained close to the ISCO for a wide range of inclinations, consistent with a rapidly spinning black hole if the source distance is typical for Galactic LMXBs. These nine observations reveal a stable, disk-dominated soft state with a weak, hot corona.
