title: The Implications of Local Fluctuations in the Galactic Midplane for Dynamical Analysis in the Gaia Era
text_ai: Orbital properties of stars, computed from their six-dimensional phase space measurements and an assumed Galactic potential, are used to understand the structure and evolution of the Galaxy. Stellar actions, computed from orbits, have the attractive quality of being invariant under certain assumptions and are therefore used as quantitative labels of a star's orbit. Here we quantify how gradients and midplane fluctuations, produced by disequilibria and corrugations, propagate into biases in Gaia phase-space labels. We construct an axisymmetric baseline potential constrained by Gaia kinematics and photometry, then superimpose locally varying midplane perturbations drawn from vertical density and velocity fields. Using torus mapping complemented by direct orbit integration, we derive actions and angles for a Gaia-like catalog, and contrast them with the fiducial, smooth-potential results. Our analysis demonstrates that midplane fluctuations of order tens of parsecs can induce systematic shifts in Jr and Jz of a few to several tens of percent for stars near the midplane, with concomitant biases in Lz and in orbital extents. The exact signature depends on the phase of the midplane wave, the vertical restoring frequency, and the star’s phase-space coordinates, leading to misclassification of resonant families and erroneous inferences about heating rates. We further show that such fluctuations can masquerade as secular trends in action-space structure, thereby contaminating measurements of radial migration and vertical heating. Mitigation strategies are proposed: (i) time-dependent, non-axisymmetric potentials guided by Gaia-derived midplane maps; (ii) joint action–angle diagnostics beyond A–space; (iii) marginalizing over plausible midplane configurations within distribution-function approaches.

title: Optimal liquidation for a risk averse investor in a one-sided limit order book driven by a Levy process
text_ai: In a one-sided limit order book, satisfying some realistic assumptions, where the unaffected price process follows a Levy process, we consider a market agent that wants to liquidate a large position of shares. We assume that the agent has constant absolute risk aversion and aims at maximising the expected utility of the cash position at the end of time. We formulate a finite-horizon stochastic control problem where the state variables are the remaining inventory, the unaffected price, and the cash account. The control is a liquidation rate compatible with a one-sided LOB, incorporating a temporary price impact and the possibility of execution through market orders. The unaffected price is modeled as a Lévy process to capture both diffusion and jumps. The objective is to maximize the expected CARA utility of the terminal cash. Using dynamic programming, we derive the HJB integro-differential equation for the value function and prove existence of a unique classical solution under standard regularity. The optimal strategy features a state-dependent boundary: when inventory exceeds the boundary, immediate liquidation is optimal; otherwise, the agent trades more gradually, balancing liquidity, impact, and jump risk.

title: Nuclear dimension and Z-stability of pure C*-algebras
text_ai: In this article I study a number of topological and algebraic dimension type properties of simple C*-algebras and their interplay. In particular, a simple C*-algebra is defined to be (tracially) (m,\bar{m})-pure, if it has (strong tracial) m-comparison and is (tracially) \bar{m}-almost divisible. These notions are related to each other, and to nuclear dimension. These results are obtained by a careful analysis of the Cuntz semigroup alongside tracial dimension theory, exploiting the interplay between m-comparison and almost divisibility to construct finite-dimensional approximations compatible with traces. We show that tracial m-comparison implies comparison by positive elements in matrix amplifications controlled by traces, while tracial \bar{m}-almost divisibility provides a robust form of internal divisibility that yields uniform decomposition therewith. Consequently, a simple nuclear C*-algebra with the stated purity has finite nuclear dimension bounded by a function d(m,\bar{m}) and, by a standard absorbing argument, satisfies A \cong A \otimes Z; i.e., Z-stability. The stable regularity statement extends to variants with nonunital or nonseparable hypotheses under natural separability and stability constraints, with a precise description of the central sequence algebra. In addition, we prove permanence under basic constructions: tensoring with strongly self-absorbing algebras preserves purity and finite nuclear dimension, and inductive limits of tracially (m,\bar{m})-pure algebras inherit the same regularity, with bounds controlled by the uniform bounds on the constituents. As a consequence, pure simple nuclear C*-algebras with finite nuclear dimension are classified by the Elliott invariant once the UCT is assumed, and they satisfy the Toms–Winter regularity properties. The framework thus clarifies the role of dimension type conditions in driving Z-stability and the modern regularity theory.

title: Towards An Efficient LLM Training Paradigm for CTR Prediction
text_ai: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated tremendous potential as the next-generation ranking-based recommendation system. Many recent works have shown that LLMs can significantly outperform conventional click-through-rate (CTR) prediction approaches. Despite such promising results, the computational inefficiency inherent in the current training paradigm makes it particularly challenging to train LLMs for ranking-based recommendation tasks on large datasets. To this end, we propose an efficient training paradigm that decouples representation learning from ranking optimization while embracing parameter-efficient fine-tuning and data-aware scheduling. We implement a modular adaptation framework in which lightweight adapters are inserted at selected transformer blocks, complemented by low-rank updates (LoRA) and, where hardware permits, quantization-aware training to shrink memory footprint without degrading signal. To cope with long-tail user histories and high-cardinality item vocabularies, we deploy a retrieval-augmented input stream that supplies compact context summaries via a lightweight retriever, thereby reducing sequence length and encoding cost while preserving ranking-relevant signals. The training objective blends a calibrated CTR ranking loss with auxiliary objectives that stabilize representation learning: a denoising masked-language objective over user and item tokens, and a contrastive alignment term that ties model representations to observed click behavior. We employ curriculum sampling that gradually increases negative sample difficulty and balances pointwise, pairwise, and listwise signals across epochs. Experiments on several public CTR benchmarks and a production-scale dataset demonstrate substantial efficiency gains: training time and peak memory consumption are reduced by up to 50–60% relative to full fine-tuning of a comparable LLM, with negligible or modest changes in AUC and log loss. Ablation studies highlight the necessity of adapters, retrieval augmentation, and the mixed objective for stable convergence.

title: Evaluation of nerve capture using classical landmarks for genicular nerve radiofrequency ablation: 3D cadaveric study.
text_ai: Radiofrequency (RF) denervation of the superolateral genicular nerve (SLGN), superomedial genicular nerve (SMGN) and inferomedial genicular nerve (IMGN) is commonly used to manage chronic knee joint pain. However, knowledge of articular branches captured, using classical landmarking techniques, remains unclear. Methods: Fifty knee specimens from ten donors (100 limbs) were prepared from fresh-frozen cadavers. Trajectories were planned using classical landmarks: the SLGN at the lateral supracondylar region, the SMGN as it curves medially near the adductor tubercle, and the IMGN along the inferomedial tibial plateau adjacent to the posteromedial corner of the tibial plateau. Under visual control, RF cannulas were advanced percutaneously to these regions, and 0.2 mL of colored latex was injected to annotate ensuing articular branches. Specimens then underwent micro-CT and high-resolution dissection to determine whether the dye co-localized with anatomically traced articular branches from the SLGN, SMGN and IMGN. A captured nerve was defined by dye presence within a genicular articular branch bearing clear continuity to the intended genicular nerve. Primary outcome was per-nerve capture rate; secondary outcomes included distance from needle tip to the nearest stained nerve, inter- and intra-specimen variability, and concordance with 3D reconstructions. Results: Per-nerve capture rates were SLGN 60% (18/30), SMGN 80% (24/30), IMGN 70% (21/30). Overall, complete triad capture occurred in 22% of specimens. Three-dimensional mapping showed that successful captures occurred when the needle tip lay within 5–7 mm of the target nerve in a near-field relationship; failures correlated with branching patterns diverting the articular supply away from the expected trunk. Variability in landmark relationships was most pronounced at the SMGN region. Conclusion: Classical landmark guidance yields moderate capture of genicular articular branches with appreciable anatomic variability. Three-dimensional analysis demonstrated a consistent proximity threshold but highlighted frequent deviations from textbook trajectories, underscoring the potential value of image-guided augmentation for optimizing nerve capture in RF ablation of the genicular nerves.

title: Loewner Theory in annulus I: evolution families and differential equations
text_ai: Loewner Theory, based on dynamical viewpoint, is a powerful tool in Complex Analysis, which plays a crucial role in such important achievements as the proof of famous Bieberbach's conjecture and well-celebrated Schramm's Stochastic Loewner Evolution (SLE). Recently Bracci et al [Bracci et al, to appear in J. Reine Angew. Math. Continuing this program, we develop a systematic theory of Loewner evolution in the annulus. We introduce the notions of evolution families and Herglotz vector fields tailored to doubly connected domains, and we formulate an annular Loewner equation driven by time–dependent vector fields. We prove that every evolution family on an annulus corresponds to a Loewner chain solving the non-autonomous differential equation, and conversely that a Loewner chain generates such a family. We establish existence and uniqueness results, regularity properties, and a Beurling–type normality criterion in terms of the associated Herglotz data. The role of the modulus of the annulus is clarified, together with boundary behavior at the inner and outer circles. Our framework sets the stage for qualitative and quantitative analysis of annular dynamics and paves the way for forthcoming stochastic extensions. as well.

title: Repeated end range spinal movement while seated abolishes the proprioceptive deficit induced by prolonged flexed sitting posture. A study assessing the statistical and clinical significance of spinal position sense.
text_ai: Sustained spinal flexion has been proposed to affect the properties of spinal tissues, increase postural muscle's activation latency and act detrimentally on proprioception. This study evaluated the effect of flexed posture (FP) on spinal proprioception and assessed the immediate effect of spinal movement on the presumable flexion-induced proprioceptive deficit. In a randomized, crossover design, twenty-four healthy adults (12 men, 12 women; mean age 24.6 ± 3.1 years) completed two sessions: a prolonged FP condition and a control neutral posture (NP) condition, each lasting 60 minutes, separated by a washout period of at least one week. Spinal proprioception was assessed with an active repositioning task using a multi-segment inclinometer system to quantify absolute error (AE) and constant error (CE) during reorientation to a standardized neutral target, applied at thoracic and lumbar levels. Assessments occurred at baseline, immediately after FP, and immediately after a brief, repeated end-range spinal movement protocol (REMS) performed seated, consisting of 12 cycles of end-range flexion-extension within a fixed chair, at a cadence of 0.25 Hz, guided by a metronome. Primary outcome was change in AE from baseline to post-FP; secondary outcomes included CE, test-retest reliability, and participant-reported comfort (0–10 numeric rating scale). Results showed a significant FP-induced deficit with AE increasing by 1.9° (95% CI 1.2–2.6; p < 0.001) and CE shifting toward flexion bias (p = 0.02). REMS abolished the deficit, with AE no longer different from baseline (p = 0.58) and effect size approaching small-to-moderate (d = 0.6). The interaction between posture and movement was significant (p < 0.01). Clinically meaningful improvements were observed in 70% of participants. These findings support a rapid, clinically relevant restoration of spinal position sense following repeated end-range spinal movement after prolonged flexed sitting. Implications for occupational and rehabilitation strategies to mitigate proprioceptive risk during sedentary work are discussed.

title: The Mystery of Two Straight Lines in Bacterial Genome Statistics. Release 2007
text_ai: In special coordinates (codon position--specific nucleotide frequencies) bacterial genomes form two straight lines in 9-dimensional space: one line for eubacterial genomes, another for archaeal genomes. All the 348 distinct bacterial genomes available in Genbank in April 2007, belong to these lines with high accuracy. The main challenge now is to explain the observed high accuracy. A plausible account is that the linearity reflects global constraints on codon-position--specific nucleotide composition imposed by the joint action of mutation pressure and translational selection on the coding repertoire. We test several explanatory routes, including (i) global GC–AT bias, (ii) codon usage patterns tied to tRNA abundance, and (iii) higher-order constraints carried by amino-acid composition. We assess robustness by resampling genes, by omitting small or highly rearranged genomes, and by cross-taxa perturbations. In every reasonable perturbation, the two lines persist with modest shifts in slope rather than disappearance, pointing to a deep, lineage-specific mutational–selective equilibrium. The findings offer a parsimonious explanation for the high explanatory power of a two-line model and suggest practical diagnostics for evolutionary and taxonomic studies based on simple linear invariants. Further work will test predictions across additional genomes.

title: MAP Estimation, Message Passing, and Perfect Graphs
text_ai: Efficiently finding the maximum a posteriori (MAP) configuration of a graphical model is an important problem which is often implemented using message passing algorithms. The optimality of such algorithms is only well established for singly-connected graphs and other limited settings. I show that for a family of models whose interaction graphs are perfect, MAP inference admits a tractable, exact solution. The key idea is to recast MAP as a maximum-weight stable set problem on an auxiliary graph, which, by perfectness, can be solved in polynomial time via established algorithms for perfect graphs. We then derive a message-passing scheme whose updates operate on maximal cliques of the base graph; on perfect graphs these updates converge to a global optimum and yield MAP configuration without exponential search. I prove that the associated linear programming relaxation is integral, establishing exactness, and provide a decomposition into local factors aligned with the clique-tree structure. The framework subsumes trees and chordal graphs and extends to graphs obtained by clique-sums of perfect subgraphs. Empirical results on synthetic datasets illustrate exactness and efficiency, outperforming solvers and matching methods on tractable instances.

title: On the ubiquity of duopolies in constant sum congestion games
text_ai: We analyse a coalition formation game between strategic service providers of a congestible service. The key novelty of our formulation is that it is a constant sum game, i.e., the total payoff across all service providers (or coalitions of providers) is fixed, and dictated by the size of the market. Within this framework, we characterize equilibrium partitions via standard coalition formation dynamics under a fixed-sum payoff vector, where each coalition’s payoff corresponds to its share of the fixed market surplus subject to network congestion. We derive conditions, in terms of latency functions and market size, under which stable partitions converge to a duopolistic structure: two coalitions capture the bulk of capacity while residual players form a fringe. We show that the constant-sum constraint induces competition that favors symmetry-breaking outcomes even when many providers are available, especially under convex congestion. We prove existence of pure Nash equilibria for standard latency classes (affine, polynomial) and obtain bounds on the price of anarchy for total welfare and for provider utilities. Numerical experiments on representative network topologies corroborate the analytics and reveal robust duopoly regimes across parameter ranges.

title: Entanglement distillation based on polarization and frequency hyperentanglement
text_ai: Entanglement distillation has many applications in quantum information processing and is an important tool for improving the quality and efficiency of quantum communication, cryptography, computing, and simulation. We propose an entanglement distillation scheme using only one pair of polarization-frequency hyperentangled photons, which can be equivalently viewed as containing two pairs of entangled logical qubits: a pair of polarization-entangled qubits and a pair of frequency-entangled qubits. By projecting the frequency degree of freedom onto a chosen basis and postselecting the corresponding polarization outcomes, the protocol realizes an effective LOCC filtering that concentrates polarization entanglement from a single hyperentangled pair. The scheme uses linear optics elements to perform a partial Bell-state measurement in the frequency subspace, followed by conditional Pauli corrections on the polarization qubits. We derive closed-form expressions for the distilled polarization fidelity Fdist and the heralding success probability Psucc as functions of the input polarization fidelity Fin and the degree of frequency entanglement. Numerical simulations for realistic SPDC parameters show that, even under phase noise in polarization, Fdist can surpass Fin with modest Psucc, enabling high-fidelity entanglement without consuming additional photon pairs. The approach is readily implementable with current polarization-frequency entangled sources and integrated photonics platforms.

title: Interpretable Data-Driven Demand Modelling for On-Demand Transit Services
text_ai: In recent years, with the advancements in information and communication technology, different emerging on-demand shared mobility services have been introduced as innovative solutions in the low-density areas, including on-demand transit (ODT), mobility on-demand (MOD) transit, and crowdsourced mobility services. However, due to their infancy, there is a strong need to understand and model the demand for these services. To this end, we propose an interpretable, data-driven framework for estimating ODT demand at high spatial-temporal resolution. The core of the approach blends interpretable statistical components with flexible machine-learning submodels to capture nonlinearities while preserving transparency to practitioners. A modular pipeline ingests multi-source data—historical trip records, zonal attributes (land use, population, employment density), network characteristics (travel time reliability, accessibility), calendar effects (holidays, events), weather, and pricing/supply indicators—and outputs zone-time demand forecasts with associated uncertainty. Demand is decomposed into additive components including baseline propensity, temporal patterns (hour-of-day, day-of-week, seasonality), spatial-context effects (urban vs. rural, proximity to transit corridors), and supply-interaction terms (vehicle availability, dispatch delay, ride-pooling propensity). We implement a hybrid modelling core that leverages generalized additive models (GAMs) to provide interpretable smooth effects and combines them with gradient-boosted trees to capture complex interactions, all cast within a Poisson or negative-binomial likelihood to account for count data properties and over-dispersion. The framework yields global and local explanations (e.g., partial effects, local feature attributions) and calibrated predictive intervals, supporting both policy evaluation and real-time operations. We demonstrate the approach on empirical ODT data from a mid-size region, benchmarking against standard Poisson and purely black-box models. Results show improved predictive accuracy, better calibration, and actionable insights for fleet sizing, zone prioritization, and dynamic routing under varying demand and supply conditions.

title: Effect of Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation on Pain Management: A Systematic Narrative Review
text_ai: Recently, clinicians have been using repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) for treating various pain conditions. This systematic narrative review aimed to examine the use and efficacy of rTMS for controlling various pain conditions. A PubMed search was conducted for articles that were published until June 7, 2019 and used rTMS for pain alleviation. Study selection yielded studies encompassing adults with neuropathic pain, fibromyalgia, musculoskeletal pain, cancer-related pain, migraine, and other chronic pain conditions. Most randomized trials employed high-frequency (5–20 Hz) stimulation of the primary motor cortex (M1) or dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), with 80–110% motor threshold, typically delivering 10–20 sessions over 2–4 weeks. Sham-controlled designs reported clinically meaningful reductions in pain intensity (measured on VAS or NRS) relative to sham in several fibromyalgia and neuropathic pain cohorts; however, effects were often modest and partially sustained up to 1–3 months. Nonrandomized and open-label studies suggested improvements in function and mood, with potential secondary benefits in sleep. EEG/fMRI correlates indicated modulation of thalamo-cortical networks. Adverse events were generally mild and transient, including localized discomfort, headaches, dizziness; serious adverse events were rare. Methodological limitations across studies included small sample sizes, short follow-up durations, variable sham conditions, and inconsistent stimulation parameters, hindering cross-study synthesis. The present review supports a cautious conclusion that rTMS may augment pain management, particularly for neuropathic and fibromyalgia pain, but standardization of protocols and rigorous multicenter trials with longer follow-up are needed to define optimal targets, doses, and durability of benefit.

title: Anticancer and cancer preventive compounds from edible marine organisms.
text_ai: A direct impact of food on health, which demonstrates that dietary habit is one of the most important determinants of chronic diseases such as cancers, has led to an increased interest of the consumers toward natural bioactive compounds as functional ingredients or nutraceuticals. Edible marine resources harbour diverse secondary metabolites with demonstrated cytotoxic activity against a spectrum of tumor models while exhibiting safe profiles in normal cells. This review synthesizes evidence on seaweeds and algae as sources of anticancer agents and cancer preventives. Key compounds include polyphenols, sulfated polysaccharides (fucoidan, ulvan, carrageenan), terpenoids and peptides, carotenoids such as fucoxanthin. The mechanisms of action are multifaceted, ranging from induction of apoptosis and cell-cycle arrest to inhibition of angiogenesis and metastasis, and modulation of oxidative stress and immune responses. The bioavailability, extraction, and standardization challenges are addressed, along with legislative and safety considerations for nutraceutical use. We highlight in vivo efficacy in rodent cancer models and, where available, human observational and interventional data, and discuss gaps, translational hurdles, and the need for clinical trials to validate edible marine compounds as complementary strategies for cancer prevention and therapy.

title: Advice Complexity of Adaptive Priority Algorithms
text_ai: The priority model was introduced to capture "greedy-like" algorithms. Motivated by the success of advice complexity in the area of online algorithms, the fixed priority model was extended to include advice, and a reduction-based framework was developed for proving lower bounds on the amount of advice required to achieve certain approximation ratios in this rather powerful model. We formalize adaptive priority algorithms (APAs) as an extension of fixed-priority, where the algorithm tailors the next priority rule to the input observed and to an advice string. We develop a reduction-based framework transferring lower bounds from string-guessing problems to APAs by constructing input families that reveal different optimal decisions late in the processing order. This yields lower bounds for broad objective classes that APAs can model. Our main results show that for several natural problems—online bipartite matching, scheduling on related machines, and packing/covering tasks expressible by monotone constraints—any APA achieving a (1+ε)-approximation requires Ω(n) bits of advice in the worst case. On the positive side, we present tight upper bounds in restricted regimes: encoding a compact blueprint of the offline optimum into O(polylog n) bits suffices for near-perfect decisions on structured instances, and O(log n) bits suffice to surpass naive greedy thresholds for many problems. We also delineate a taxonomy of advice types and their effects, distinguishing order-guidance from content-guidance, and show a clear separation between pure online behavior, fixed-priority with advice, and adaptive strategies. These results chart when advice is essential to circumvent adaptivity and when it remains fruitless.

title: Self-Refine Instruction-Tuning for Aligning Reasoning in Language Models
text_ai: The alignments of reasoning abilities between smaller and larger Language Models are largely conducted via Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) using demonstrations generated from robust Large Language Models (LLMs). Although these approaches deliver more performant models, they do not show sufficiently strong generalization ability as the training only relies on the provided demonstrations. To address this, we introduce Self-Refine Instruction-Tuning (SRIT), a lightweight augmentation to standard SFT that orchestrates an internal self-improvement loop over demonstrations. The model first generates solutions with explicit reasoning traces. A self-critique module then analyzes those traces to identify logical gaps, hallucinated inferences, and misaligned abstractions, producing revised demonstrations and corrected instructions. These refined exemplars are incorporated into subsequent instruction-tuning rounds, creating a progressively more robust alignment between instruction-following and reasoning behavior. Importantly, SRIT leverages only the model’s own outputs, avoiding dependence on external evaluators or adversarial data. We validate SRIT on a spectrum of tasks with increasing reasoning complexity and distribution shift. Across benchmarks, SRIT yields superior generalization to unseen task families, better coherence and calibration of reasoning steps, and lower failure rates relative to standard SFT baselines, while maintaining comparable compute.

title: Development and clinical study of submicronic-atropine sulphate respiratory fluid as a novel organophosphorous poisoning antidote.
text_ai: Increased use of organophosphate insecticides (OPI) and possibility of terror groups using stocks of nerve agents underscore the need to develop effective and safe antidotes. While intramuscular administration of antidotes like atropine sulphate (AS) has certain lacunae, intravenous route may not be always feasible in emergency field conditions. In the present work, SAS-RF was optimized for aerosol performance and clinical usability. The inhalation fluid, prepared under sterile conditions, yielded submicronic droplets with a mean aerodynamic diameter near 0.9 µm and a span below 1.6, enabling deep lung deposition while minimizing oropharyngeal losses. In vitro rheological and stability assessments demonstrated no significant aggregation for 6 months at 4–25°C. Pharmacokinetic profiling in healthy volunteers (n=20) showed a rapid rise in plasma atropine within 2–4 minutes post-inhalation, a Cmax in the low ng/mL range reached within minutes, and a terminal half-life compatible with repeated dosing if required. In a Phase I/II open-label cohort (n=12) of adults with mild OP exposure, SAS-RF produced rapid attenuation of bronchorrhea, bronchospasm, and bradycardia within 5–10 minutes, with most subjects avoiding parenteral atropine and without injection-related complications. Safety comparisons with standard IM atropine indicated similar tolerability but with markedly improved field practicality and patient comfort. Pharmacodynamic data showed suppression of muscarinic signs aligned with serum levels within the therapeutic window. Collectively, these findings support progression to larger, controlled field trials and suggest SAS-RF as a readily deployable antidote for acute OP poisoning, with potential applicability in agricultural settings and mass-exposure scenarios where intravenous access is impractical.
prefix: Increased use of organophosphate insecticides (OPI) and possibility of terror groups using stocks of nerve agents underscore the need to develop effective and safe antidotes. While intramuscular administration of antidotes like atropine sulphate (AS) has certain lacunae, intravenous route may not be always feasible in emergency field conditions.

title: Quantum secret sharing for a multipartite system under energy dissipation
text_ai: We propose a protocol for multipartite secret sharing of quantum information through an \textit{amplitude damping} quantum channel. This network is, for example, of two organizations communicating with their own employees connected via classical channels locally. We consider a GHZ state distributed among four members in an asymmetric fashion where the members of a sub-party collaborate to decode the received information at their end. After distribution, each qubit traverses an amplitude damping channel with parameter γ, producing a mixed four-qubit state that retains a GHZ component. The decoding step relies on LOCC that couple stabilizer measurements with conditional feeds, enabling the reconstruction of the encoded secret only when at least one member from each sub-party collaborates. This (2,2) threshold realization preserves secrecy against unilateral attacks and exploits residual correlations preserved under dissipation. We derive analytical expressions for the recovered secret fidelity F(γ), the reconstruction probability P_rec(γ), and the achievable secret-sharing rate R(γ) as functions of γ and the chosen measurement scheme. Numerical simulations for loss profiles corroborate that the quantum advantage persists up to a critical γc and outperforms secret sharing under comparable energy constraints.

title: An Oka principle for equivariant isomorphisms
text_ai: Let $G$ be a reductive complex Lie group acting holomorphically on normal Stein spaces $X$ and $Y$, which are locally $G$-biholomorphic over a common categorical quotient $Q$. When is there a global $G$-biholomorphism $X\to Y$? Let Aut_G(X_q) denote the group of G-biholomorphisms of the fibre X_q that commute with the quotient map X_q → Q. A local G-biholomorphism over overlaps provides a Čech cocycle with values in the sheaf of holomorphic Aut_G(X_q)-valued maps on Q, hence an obstruction class [c] ∈ H^1(Q, Aut_G(X_q)). The main result can be stated as follows. Theorem (Oka principle for equivariant isomorphisms). Suppose X and Y are normal Stein G-manifolds, locally G-biholomorphic over a common categorical quotient Q, and suppose the associated cocycle of local G-biholomorphisms defines a class [c] in H^1(Q, Aut_G(X_q)) which vanishes. Then there exists a global G-biholomorphism X → Y over Q. Moreover, this global isomorphism can be obtained by deforming any given continuous (or smooth) G-equivariant isomorphism through a holomorphic path in the space of G-biholomorphisms, i.e., the problem satisfies a parametric Oka principle: every holomorphic family of local isomorphisms over a Stein parameter space S can be extended to a holomorphic family over S. Consequences and remarks. The theorem reduces the global existence of X ≅_G Y to the vanishing of a topological obstruction on Q, and when this obstruction is absent, the holomorphic gluing is guaranteed by the Oka property of the sheaf of equivariant automorphisms. The parametric version yields holomorphic moduli for equivariant isomorphisms, with applications to linearization problems and to the classification of G-actions on Stein spaces up to equivariant biholomorphism.

title: MVGrasp: Real-Time Multi-View 3D Object Grasping in Highly Cluttered Environments
text_ai: Nowadays robots play an increasingly important role in our daily life. In human-centered environments, robots often encounter piles of objects, packed items, or isolated objects. Therefore, a robot must be able to grasp and manipulate different objects in various situations to help humans with daily tasks. MVGrasp integrates synchronized multi-view RGB-D sensing with a fast voxel-based fusion to produce a high-fidelity 3D representation of the workspace. A learned grasp sampler proposes robust 6-DOF grasps conditioned on local geometry and occlusion masks, and a geometric verifier validates candidates by simulating approach trajectories to avoid collisions. The planner selects grasps with minimal approach distance and high success probability, enabling single-shot execution in clutter. We implement a real-time pipeline on commodity hardware using parallel GPU inference and CPU-based collision checking, achieving sub-50 ms perception per frame and grasp inference within 90 ms, enabling loop rates over 10 Hz. We evaluate on a diverse set of objects, including deformables, rigid symmetric, and small items, across piles, shelves, and isolated targets. MVGrasp outperforms state-of-the-art single-view methods in cluttered scenes, with increased success rate and reduced planning time, demonstrating generalization and operation in cluttered environments.

Therefore, a robot must be able to grasp and manipulate different objects in various situations to help humans with daily tasks.

title: A tutorial on individualized treatment effect prediction from randomized trials with a binary endpoint
text_ai: Randomized trials typically estimate average relative treatment effects, but decisions on the benefit of a treatment are possibly better informed by more individualized predictions of the absolute treatment effect. In case of a binary outcome, these predictions of absolute individualized treatment effect require knowledge of the individual's risk without treatment and incorporation of a possibly differential treatment effect (i.e. i.e., treatment effect heterogeneity) across covariates. The absolute individualized treatment effect is the risk difference RD(X) = p1(X) − p0(X), where p0(X) denotes the untreated risk conditional on X and p1(X) the risk under treatment. The tutorial presents a practical workflow to identify and estimate such effects from randomized trials with a binary endpoint. We first state estimands that are identifiable under randomization and discuss the implications of scale (absolute vs. relative effects) for interpretation. We then summarize estimation strategies: (i) plug-in approaches that fit models for Y|T,X to obtain p0(X) and p1(X) and hence RD(X); (ii) direct or uplift approaches that target the conditional treatment effect without requiring correct specification of both potential risks (e.g., causal forests, interaction models, or other machine‑learning–based estimators). For each method we cover implementation details, model selection, and validation, including cross-validation, sample splitting, and diagnostics for calibration and discrimination. Inference is addressed via bootstrap or asymptotic variance estimates, with attention to finite‑sample uncertainty and issues such as non‑collapsibility of odds ratios on the logistic scale. The tutorial concludes with guidance on reporting individualized predicted benefits, presenting decision thresholds, and integrating these predictions into trial reports and patient‑facing decision aids.

title: SensatUrban: Learning Semantics from Urban-Scale Photogrammetric Point Clouds
text_ai: With the recent availability and affordability of commercial depth sensors and 3D scanners, an increasing number of 3D (i.e., RGBD, point cloud) datasets have been publicized to facilitate research in 3D computer vision. However, existing datasets either cover relatively small areas or have limited semantic annotations. To address these limitations, we introduce SensatUrban, a large-scale photogrammetric point cloud dataset spanning multiple urban districts and captured under diverse architectural typologies. Data are produced with a full photogrammetric pipeline (dense image acquisition, structure‑from‑motion, multi‑view stereo) and yield dense, colorized, metrically registered point clouds over several square kilometers. We provide comprehensive semantic annotations at the point level, organized in a hierarchical taxonomy including buildings, roads, pavements, vegetation, water, vehicles, pedestrians, rail infrastructure, signage, fences, and miscellaneous urban objects. Ground-truth labels were obtained through meticulous manual annotation with validation against auxiliary sources and inter‑annotator agreement checks. Standardized train/validation/test splits and an explicit evaluation protocol (mean IoU, per-class IoU, precision/recall) are released. Baseline experiments with representative 3D architectures demonstrate the dataset’s utility for urban semantic understanding and highlight remaining challenges such as scale, class imbalance, and label noise inherent to photogrammetric data.

title: Beyond Uncertainty: Evidential Deep Learning for Robust Video Temporal Grounding
text_ai: Existing Video Temporal Grounding (VTG) models excel in accuracy but often overlook open-world challenges posed by open-vocabulary queries and untrimmed videos. This leads to unreliable predictions for noisy, corrupted, and out-of-distribution data. Adapting VTG models to dynamically estimate uncertainties based on user input can address this issue. To this end, we present an evidential VTG framework attaching an evidential head to the text encoder and the temporal proposal network, producing Dirichlet parameters α over temporal proposals. Ground-truth intervals are learned with a supervised regression objective augmented by an evidential consistency term that discourages overconfidence on uncertain or out-of-distribution queries. The model yields a principled uncertainty estimate—epistemic (model) and aleatoric (data) via the total evidence α0 = ∑ αk and the derived uncertainty U = K/α0. At inference, high U triggers abstention or a coarser proposal, improving robustness in untrimmed inputs. We introduce a data-augmentation strategy and curriculum exposing the model to corruptions and novel terms. Extensive experiments on open-world VTG benchmarks demonstrate improved accuracy under noise and OOD queries, with reliable uncertainty calibration and actionable abstention behavior without sacrificing in-distribution performance.

This leads to unreliable predictions for noisy, corrupted, and out-of-distribution data. Adapting VTG models to dynamically estimate uncertainties based on user input can address this issue.

title: Moist convection is most vigorous at intermediate atmospheric humidity
text_ai: In Earth's current climate, moist convective updraft speeds increase with surface warming. This trend suggests that very vigorous convection might be the norm in extremely hot and humid atmospheres, such as those undergoing a runaway greenhouse transition. Here, we show that, at fixed sea-surface temperature, the peak in vertical velocity and convective mass flux shifts nonlinearly with environmental relative humidity. In a suite of cloud-resolving simulations spanning surface temperatures from 290 to 340 K and column RH from dry to saturated, updraft speeds initially rise with warming but plateau and eventually decline as humidity approaches saturation. The maximum becomes pronounced at intermediate humidity, with peak updraft speeds exceeding those at both lower and higher RH for the same Ts. This non-monotonic behavior is robust to changes in microphysical parameterizations and entrainment rate formulations. The mechanism is a competition between latent-heat release, which enhances buoyancy of rising parcels, and entrainment of ambient air, which tends to cool and desaturate plumes. At very dry environments, insufficient moisture limits condensation and CAPE; at very moist environments, the buoyancy advantage from latent heating is offset by near-saturated environmental lapse rates and stronger entrainment of moist air, which dampens buoyancy contrasts and increases dilution. At intermediate humidity, condensation efficiency is high enough to maximize latent-energy feedback while entrainment remains moderate, yielding the largest vertical velocities and mass fluxes. These results imply a ceiling on convective vigor in runaway-like climates and suggest that mid-humidity atmospheres may host the most intense convection, with consequences for precipitation efficiency, cloud radiative forcing, and the interpretation of exoplanet climates.

title: Current irritability robustly related to current and prior anxiety in bipolar disorder.
text_ai: Although current irritability and current/prior anxiety have been associated in unipolar depression, these relationships are less well understood in bipolar disorder (BD). We investigated relationships between current irritability and current/prior anxiety as well as other current emotions and BD illness characteristics. Methods: In a cross-sectional sample of adults with bipolar I or II disorder (n ≈ 200), recruited from clinics and research registries, we examined associations among current irritability, current anxiety, and prior anxiety, alongside a range of current emotions and illness characteristics. Current irritability and emotions were assessed with validated scales; lifetime anxiety disorders and onset were determined via structured interview. We used hierarchical regression to test whether current state anxiety and lifetime anxiety predicted irritability beyond depressive and manic symptom severity, mood burden, sex, age, and BD subtype; we also tested persistence after adjustment for general negative affect. Results: Current irritability showed robust positive associations with both current-state anxiety and lifetime anxiety history (p < .05 to .001) that remained after controlling for depressive (MADRS) and manic (YMRS) severity. Among emotions, anger and sadness related to irritability, but anxiety had the strongest link. Prior anxiety contributed unique variance to irritability beyond concurrent symptoms, indicating a lasting vulnerability. Patterns were similar in BD I and BD II, with some variation tied to episode history and cumulative mood burden. Sensitivity analyses excluding substance-use comorbidity yielded concordant results. Conclusions: In BD, irritability is tightly linked to both current and prior anxiety rather than being a mere reflection of current mood. Targeting anxiety processes may attenuate irritability and improve functioning.

title: Quasar Photometric Redshifts and Candidate Selection: A New Algorithm Based on Optical and Mid-Infrared Photometric Data
text_ai: We present a new algorithm to estimate quasar photometric redshifts (photo-$z$s), by considering the asymmetries in the relative flux distributions of quasars. The relative flux models are built with multivariate Skew-t distributions in the multi-dimensional space of relative fluxes as a function of redshift and magnitude. Estimating photo-zs is performed via a likelihood-based framework that integrates the skew-t relative flux models with measurement uncertainties and non-detections, yielding a posterior distribution P(z | data) and a quasar class probability P_Q. The model is trained on a diverse spectroscopic sample drawn from SDSS/BOSS/eBOSS and complemented by matched WISE photometry to exploit optical–mid-IR color space where quasar colors separate more cleanly from stellar and galactic contaminants. Relative fluxes are constructed with respect to carefully chosen reference bands to minimize calibration systematics, and the skew-t components capture asymmetric tails arising from emission-line variability, intrinsic spectral-energy-distribution diversity, and host-galaxy contribution in low-redshift quasars. The framework naturally accommodates censoring due to non-detections by incorporating upper-limit information in the likelihood. We evaluate performance against leading template-fitting and machine-learning photo-z approaches. For a broad redshift range 0.3 < z < 5 and i-band magnitudes up to ≈21.5, we obtain a scatter of NMAD ≈ 0.05–0.09 with an outlier fraction of a few percent (|Δz|/(1+z) > 0.15). Mean residuals are near zero for high-P_Q selections, indicating minimal bias. The inclusion of MIR data notably reduces degeneracies at z ≈ 1–2.5 and z ≈ 3, particularly for reddened quasars, while maintaining robustness in the presence of photometric noise. The method provides full P(z) densities and probabilistic quasar-vs-non-quasar classifications, enabling optimized target selection for spectroscopic follow-up and improved quasar clustering analyses in large-scale structure studies. We release the catalogues of photo-zs, P(z), and candidate flags for community use.

The relative flux models are built with multivariate Skew-t distributions in the multi-dimensional space of relative fluxes as a function of redshift and magnitude.

title: Exploiting Qubit Reuse through Mid-circuit Measurement and Reset
text_ai: Quantum measurement is important to quantum computing as it extracts the outcome of the circuit at the end of the computation. Previously, all measurements have to be done at the end of the circuit. Otherwise, it will incur significant errors. But it is not the case now. Mid-circuit measurement and reset enable the deliberate projection of intermediate qubits into classical bits and their immediate reuse in subsequent stages. We present a framework that integrates high-fidelity, fast-reset operations with reliable mid-circuit readout, supported by real-time classical control. By partitioning algorithms into measurement-conditional blocks, our approach reduces circuit depth while preserving final outcomes. The method relies on calibrated resets to ground or to designated states, with measurement outcomes stored in classical registers and used to steer forthcoming gates via feed-forward. We demonstrate a protocol for reusing qubits across multiple subcircuits in benchmark circuits, achieving substantial resource reductions in simulated devices. Across representative tasks, we observe depth reductions and qubit-count savings while maintaining comparable end-to-end fidelity. An error-analysis reveals favorable performance in moderate-noise regimes, and we discuss hardware considerations for scaling mid-circuit measurement to larger architectures.

title: A probabilistic reduced-order modeling framework for patient-specific cardio-mechanical analysis
text_ai: Cardio-mechanical models can be used to support clinical decision-making. Unfortunately, the substantial computational effort involved in many cardiac models hinders their application in the clinic, despite the fact that they may provide valuable information. In this work, we present a probabilistic reduced-order modeling (ROM) framework to dramatically reduce the computational effort of such models while providing a credibility interval. To this end, we develop a probabilistic ROM that couples a physics-based reduced-order surrogate with a Bayesian inference engine to deliver not only point predictions but also credible intervals for clinically relevant quantities. The spatial ROM relies on a POD-Galerkin reduction of a high-fidelity finite-element model of the ventricle, augmented with a parametric activation law and an anisotropic constitutive description of myocardial tissue. The reduced basis is constructed from an archive of high-fidelity simulations spanning plausible ranges of patient- and pathology-specific parameters (stiffness, fiber orientation, pre-/afterload, and activation timing). A stochastic surrogate maps the reduced coefficients and uncertain inputs to outputs of interest (wall stresses, regional strains, cavity volumes) and is equipped with priors that reflect physiological plausibility. Bayesian calibration uses patient data (e.g., cine and tagged MRI, invasively measured pressures) to update posterior distributions over the uncertain quantities, yielding posterior predictive distributions for targets such as peak systolic strain, wall thickening, and stress hotspots. Uncertainty propagation is performed via Monte Carlo sampling in the reduced space or via a stochastic Galerkin approach, enabling explicit credibility intervals on predictions. We demonstrate substantial computational savings (nearly two to three orders of magnitude) while maintaining accuracy within clinically acceptable tolerances across synthetic benchmarks and retrospective patient studies. The framework supports online data assimilation for sequentially acquired measurements, enabling real-time decision support for diagnosis, therapy planning, and device optimization.

title: Deriving approximation tolerance constraints from verification runs
text_ai: Approximate computing (AC) is an emerging paradigm for energy-efficient computation. The basic idea of AC is to sacrifice high precision for low energy by allowing for hardware which only carries out "approximately correct" calculations. For software verification, this challenges the validity of verification results for programs run on approximate hardware. Here, we present a methodology to derive approximation tolerance constraints (ATCs) from verification runs. ATCs are formal guarantees that bounds on numerical deviation do not compromise verified properties. We instrument verification runs to record, for each program construct, the observed error relative to a reference exact execution. A post-hoc analysis computes admissible error budgets expressed as constraints over inputs, states, and control-flow, which are then composed to yield module-level tolerances. We propagate these through a simple yet expressive model of the approximate hardware, deriving a schedulable set of AC settings that satisfy all ATCs. Our pipeline supports both worst-case and probabilistic guarantees under realistic input distributions. We validate on a suite of benchmarks and several approximate cores, showing that the derived ATCs enable energy reductions while preserving safety and correctness with confidence across diverse domains.

title: Nonlinear fractional waves at elastic interfaces
text_ai: We derive the nonlinear fractional surface wave equation that governs compression waves at an interface that is coupled to a viscous bulk medium. The fractional character of the differential equation comes from the fact that the effective thickness of the bulk layer that is coupled to the interface is frequency dependent. Enforcing compatibility of the interfacial displacement with the bulk velocity field and eliminating bulk degrees of freedom yields a closed equation for the interfacial compression. The viscous bulk contributes a memory kernel that decays as a fractional power, imparting a Caputo derivative in time. The resulting equation captures both dispersion and nonlinearity: the fractional time derivative governs rate-dependent attenuation, while higher-order spatial derivatives encode dispersion from the finite coupling thickness. The nonlinear term, from the interface's elastic contrast, yields cubic and higher-order nonlinearity. We show that the fractional order is determined by μ, ρ and the effective coupling length ℓ_eff(ω). In the weakly nonlinear regime, a reductive perturbation yields a fractional KdV-type envelope equation and supports modulated wave packets with algebraic tails. The framework unifies classical surface acoustics with fractional dissipation and provides measurable signatures for experiments.

title: A Virtual Quantum Network Prototype for Open Access
text_ai: The rise of quantum networks has revolutionized domains such as communication, sensing, and cybersecurity. Despite this progress, current quantum network systems remain limited in scale, are highly application-specific (e.g., for quantum key distribution), and lack a clear road map for global expansion. To address these constraints, we introduce a Virtual Quantum Network Prototype (VQNP) designed as an open-access platform that emulates a heterogeneous quantum layer atop conventional networking. The prototype decouples quantum hardware from control logic, enabling researchers to prototype protocols and topologies without direct access to devices. Its modular stack comprises a quantum abstraction layer, a virtual fabric of nodes, and orchestration plane governed by software-defined control framework. The design supports multiple quantum modalities—discrete qubits, continuous-variable channels, and entanglement distribution—while interfacing with classical networks via standardized timing models and APIs. We evaluate the prototype with synthetic workloads and traces, reporting metrics such as end-to-end latency, entanglement fidelity, secret-key rates, and resource utilization across topologies. By providing reproducible experiments, tutorials, and data repositories, the project lowers entry barriers, invites cross-disciplinary experimentation, and informs routing, caching, and provisioning policies for future networks.

title: Quantum Kinetic Theory of Thermoelectric and Thermal Transport in a Magnetic Field
text_ai: We present a general quantum kinetic theory that accounts for the interplay between a temperature gradient, momentum-space Berry curvatures of Bloch electrons, and Bloch-state scattering. Using a theory that incorporates the presence of a temperature gradient by introducing a "thermal vector potential", we derive a quantum kinetic equation for Bloch electrons in the presence of disorder and a temperature gradient. We obtain closed-form expressions for the linear response of electric and heat currents to a temperature gradient and electric field in the presence of a magnetic field, decomposed into intrinsic Berry-curvature contributions, side-jump and skew-scattering corrections, and conventional drift terms. The formalism yields a quantum kinetic equation whose collision integral preserves particle number and encodes momentum-relaxing processes. Solving in the relaxation-time approximation and beyond, we show that the transverse (Nernst) and longitudinal thermoelectric coefficients acquire corrections that are odd under time reversal and controlled by the Berry curvature dipole in momentum space. In a weak-field regime, we recover the Mott relation between thermoelectric coefficients and the energy derivative of the conductivity, generalized to include Berry-phase corrections. The theory also predicts a quantum limitation to the Wiedemann–Franz law in regions where Berry curvature and disorder compete with Landau quantization. As an application, we analyze a two-dimensional electron gas with finite Berry curvature and a perpendicular magnetic field, highlighting the interplay between intrinsic anomalous contributions and conventional Landau-level physics. Our results unify disparate approaches to quantum thermoelectric transport and provide a framework to interpret experiments on topological materials, magnetic semiconductors, and moiré systems under thermal gradients.

title: Saving Science by Doing Less of It?
text_ai: In the current issue of The New Atlantis, Daniel Sarewitz, professor of science and society at Arizona State University, argues that science is broken because it is managed and judged by scientists themselves, operating under Vannevar Bush's famous 1945 declaration that scientific progress depends on the "free play of free intellects … dictated by their curiosity." Building on Sarewitz's diagnosis, this paper examines how incentive and governance structures—publish-or-perish culture, competitive grants, and field-centric hierarchies—shape research agendas, often at the expense of rigor and social relevance. Drawing on policy scholarship and illustrative cases, I argue that modest, principled restraint can improve science's returns to society without dampening curiosity. The core proposition is to realign incentives toward quality, reproducibility, and problem-solving, rather than sheer novelty or volume. A concrete reform agenda is proposed: (1) cap or re-balance funding streams to reduce redundancy and overextension; (2) expand support for replication, negative results, and robust data infrastructure; (3) couple outcomes with external evaluation and broader stakeholder input; (4) pilot mission-informed programs with sunset reviews to prevent mission creep. While acknowledging risks—reduced experimentation, potential chilling effects—the framework aims to preserve scientific autonomy while strengthening accountability and public trust. The overarching claim is that strategic restraint can save science by doing less of it more effectively.

title: Graphene field effect transistors as room-temperature Terahertz detectors
text_ai: The unique optoelectronic properties of graphene [1] make it an ideal platform for a variety of photonic applications [2], including fast photodetectors [3], transparent electrodes [4], optical modulators [5], and ultra-fast lasers [6]. In this work, we explore graphene field-effect transistors (GFETs) as room-temperature detectors for Terahertz (THz) radiation. We combine device engineering with a broad characterization routine to elucidate the dominant rectification and photothermoelectric mechanisms that enable THz responsivity in the absence of an external bias. By leveraging the ambipolar transport and high carrier mobility of graphene, GFETs are operated in a regime where plasmon-assisted absorption and bolometric effects contribute synergistically to a measurable photoresponse. We report a comprehensive set of measurements including frequency-resolved responsivity, noise characterization, and time-domain response, demonstrating a rapid, sub-nanosecond temporal latency and high signal-to-noise performance up to several hundreds of gigahertz. Our results reveal that device geometry, contact engineering, and substrate choice critically influence coupling to THz fields and the ensuing photogenerated carrier dynamics. Through systematic variation of gate voltage and source–drain bias, we identify optimal operating points that maximize responsivity while suppressing dark current. The demonstrated room-temperature operation, compatibility with on-chip integration, and scalable fabrication routes underscore the potential of GFET-based THz detectors for imaging, spectroscopy, and communication systems.

title: A Feedback Neural Network for Small Target Motion Detection in Cluttered Backgrounds
text_ai: Small target motion detection is critical for insects to search for and track mates or prey which always appear as small dim speckles in the visual field. A class of specific neurons, called small target motion detectors (STMDs), has been characterized by exquisite sensitivity for small target motion. Recent work has revealed that STMD responses can be shaped by feedback interactions within their microcircuits, enabling more robust discrimination of targets from clutter and noise. Here, we present a computational model—A Feedback Neural Network for Small Target Motion Detection in Cluttered Backgrounds (FFN-STMD)—that integrates feedforward contrast sensitivity with recurrent modulatory pathways. The architecture comprises a retinotopically organized ensemble of feature detectors, delayed coincidence units, and a top-down feedback loop that dynamically adapts gain and suppression according to local motion statistics. Our key contribution is a biologically inspired feedback mechanism that enhances target saliency when a coherent small object traverses a textured background, while suppressing spurious responses to background flow and noise. We evaluate FFN-STMD on synthetic and real-world sequences, demonstrating improved detection accuracy, reduced false positives, and lower latency relative to purely feedforward STMD-inspired models. The results suggest that feedback control can endow small target detectors with greater resilience in cluttered environments, offering insights for both neuroethological studies and autonomous vision systems.

title: The Community In-reach Rehabilitation and Care Transition (CIRACT) clinical and cost-effectiveness randomisation controlled trial in older people admitted to hospital as an acute medical emergency.
text_ai: To compare the clinical and cost-effectiveness of a Community In-reach Rehabilitation and Care Transition (CIRACT) service with the traditional hospital-based rehabilitation (THB-Rehab) service. Pragmatic randomised controlled trial with an integral health economic study. Large UK teaching hospital, with community follow-up. Frail older people aged 70 years and older admitted to hospital as an acute medical emergency. The primary outcome is the composite incidence of functional decline and unplanned readmission within 90 days of randomisation, assessed using validated activity of daily living scales and hospital episode statistics. Secondary outcomes include quality of life (as measured by a generic instrument suitable for older adults), cognitive function, mood, independence in activities of daily living, discharge destination, length of index admission, and 12-month mortality. Economic evaluation will adopt a societal perspective, capturing health and social care costs, informal caregiver time, and patient out-of-pocket expenses, with cost-effectiveness expressed as incremental cost per quality-adjusted life-year gained. A process evaluation will explore fidelity, acceptability, and mechanisms of action, incorporating stakeholder interviews with participants, carers, primary and secondary care staff, and CIRACT team members. Participants are randomised to receive either CIRACT, a home-based, multi-disciplinary rehabilitation and transitional care model delivered through liaison with community services and primary care, or THB-Rehab, the standard inpatient rehabilitation pathway requiring predominantly hospital-based therapy and subsequent discharge planning. Follow-up assessments are conducted at 3, 6, and 12 months post-randomisation, with blinded outcome assessment where feasible. The trial is designed to detect a clinically meaningful difference in functional status and a favorable cost-effectiveness profile for CIRACT, while ensuring equity across diverse socioeconomic and clinical subgroups. Implications extend to policy on post-acute care delivery for older adults, aiming to optimise recovery trajectories, reduce unnecessary hospital stay, and enhance community-based support networks.

title: Effectiveness of Bone Conduction Stimulation Applied Directly to the Otic Capsule Measured at Promontory: Assessment in Cadavers.
text_ai: The aims of this study included: (a) to develop a method of direct acoustic bone conduction (BC) stimulation applied directly to the otic capsule, (b) to investigate the effect of different stimulation sites on the promontory displacement amplitude, and (c) to find the best stimulation site (among 2 located directly on the otic capsule and 1 standard site approved for clinical use) that provides the greatest transmission of vibratory energy. A controlled cadaveric experimental design was employed. Fresh human temporal bones (n = 8) were prepared with preservation of the otic capsule and promontory, and microphone-free vibrational excitation was delivered using a calibrated tactile transducer positioned at three sites: two sites directly on the otic capsule (superior and inferior to the promontory) and one conventional clinical reference site on the skull. Promontory displacement was quantified with a high-sensitivity laser Doppler vibrometer, ensuring minimal mounting artefacts and environmental noise. Stimulation amplitudes spanned clinically relevant ranges, and responses were normalized to input force to yield displacement transfer functions. Reproducibility across specimens and intersite comparisons were analyzed using repeated-measures ANOVA and post hoc pairwise testing with Bonferroni correction. Results demonstrated statistically significant differences in promontory response among stimulation sites, with direct otic capsule locations yielding greater displacement transfer than the standard clinical site, particularly at mid-to-high frequencies (1–4 kHz). The superior otic capsule site produced the largest average promontory displacements across the frequency spectrum, though the inferior capsule site approached this magnitude at lower frequencies (0.5–1 kHz). The standard reference site, while providing consistent activation, generated the smallest promontory responses overall. The findings indicate that direct BC stimulation applied to the otic capsule can enhance vibratory energy transmission to the cochlear promontory, suggesting potential gains in audibility for conductive and mixed hearing loss paradigms when delivered via direct otic capsule contact. Limitations include cadaveric tissue properties and the absence of middle-ear feedback; translational work in living subjects is warranted to confirm perceptual correlates and safety.
